utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner, Daryl Mundis and our case manager, Andres Vatter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we have the appearances for the other Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the Trial Chamber I would like to greet everyone present, members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, the accused and everyone else present in the courtroom. As you are aware, we will be hearing two witnesses today. Thanks to the registrar, we will have a hearing this morning which will go on until 2.00 p.m.. We will have a one-hour break so that everyone can have a rest, and we will resume at 3.00 p.m. and continue until 4.30. We expect to conclude the hearing at 4.30, unless it's necessary to continue for a little extra time. So roughly speaking, this is how we will proceed today. If there are no issues to raise, we will call the witness into the courtroom immediately. Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before the witness enters the courtroom, you've already said that we should deal with all the documents that have to be admitted into evidence, and as a result, I would like to tender into evidence the Defence documents that were shown to the witness yesterday. Yesterday, Defence counsel showed Mr. Mesanovic documents that had to do with the relation between the army and the HVO and then there were other documents and some documents that have already been admitted. We now suggest that given that the witness has recognised the documents, either as documents that he -- either as documents compiled by the Municipal Staff or documents signed by his commander from the Municipal Staff or recognised them as documents, the contents of which were familiar to him or they were documents in which the events described were familiar to him either because he participated in these events or was familiar with these events given the position that he held, I therefore suggest that documents from section 1, the following, be accepted, admitted 0513, 0823, 0824, 0843, 0846, 0856, 0868, 0902. Defence counsel didn't show the witness document 1032 because this is a document which was put in the binder by mistake and has nothing to do with the area of Travnik, which is why at this moment in time Defence counsel won't be tendering this document into evidence. In addition, we suggest the following documents be admitted into evidence, documents from section 2 contained in our binder. These are the following documents: 0530, 0656, 0708, 0853, 0880, 0912. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we have 14 documents to deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The first document under section 1 is DH513, the English version will be DH513/E; DH823, the English version will be DH823/E; the following document DH824, and the English version DH824/E; DH843, the English version will be DH843/E; DH846, the English version will be DH846/E; DH856; the English version will be DH856/E; DH868, the English version will be DH868/E; DH902, the English version will be DH902/E. And now as far as section 2 is concerned: DH530, the English version will be DH530/E; DH656, English version will be DH656/E; DH708, the English version will be DH708/E; DH853, the English version will be DH853/E; DH880, the English version will be DH880/E; and finally DH912, the English version will be DH912/E. And I'd also like to add that the document tendered into evidence under DH931 yesterday will be DH931 for the English version. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We are -- we have dealt with everything. All the motions have been dealt with, all the documents have been tendered, so we are entirely up-to-date. There are no backlogs. Could the usher now call the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you can hear what I'm saying in your own language since you should be receiving the interpretation. If so, please say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have been called here as a witness for the Defence. You will be testifying about events in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993. Before you take the solemn declaration, I'd like to ask you to tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ribo Haso. I was born on the 25th of February, 1956, in Kljaci village in the Travnik municipality, in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What is your current Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond profession? Are you employed at the moment or are you retired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm the chief of the administration for defence in Zenica canton. It's the Federal Ministry for Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In 1992 and 1993, what position did you hold, or if you were a member of the military, did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, I was a member of the Territorial Defence in Travnik municipality. Up until the 1st of June, I was the chief of staff, and afterwards, until the 18th of November, I was the commander of the Travnik Municipal Staff. Afterwards, from the 18th to the 20th of November, 1993, I was the commander of the 301st Mechanised Brigade, and my rank was captain first class.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before a national court or -- a national court about the events in 1992 and 1993 or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time, here in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but have you testified before a national court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now ask the usher to show the text of the solemn declaration. Could you read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Defence counsel for their examination-in-chief, I'd like to supply you with some information about the procedure that will be followed here. This is what I do whenever a witness appears before the Chamber. This is in order to clarify the procedure. First you will have to answer questions that will be put to you by Defence counsel. They are to your left. When they have concluded their examination-in-chief, members of the Prosecution, over to your right, will conduct their cross-examination. At the end of their cross-examination, Defence counsel may ask you additional questions if necessary. According to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, the three Judges sitting before you may ask you questions at any point in time if we feel that this is necessary, either in order to clarify some of your answers or because we believe that there are certain gaps that should be filled. As a rule, we ask questions at the end of the examination and cross-examination, but we can ask questions at any point in time. It's also possible that we might not have any questions to ask you. If a question is not clear to you or if you find that the question is difficult, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it to be sure that you have understood the question well and to make sure that your answer is a clear one. The procedure we follow here is an oral procedure, and it is also based on the documents that will be shown to you by Defence counsel and perhaps by the Prosecution, and sometimes if the Judges put questions to witnesses, they may show the witness exhibits in order to support the questions put. Since you have taken the solemn declaration, you shouldn't give false testimony. As you're well aware, giving false testimony is an offence which could be punished by a prison sentence. Since you are a former member of the military and commander of the 301st Mechanised Brigade, you should be aware of the fact that when answering a question, if your answer contains elements that might be used against you in some other case, you should be aware of the fact that you have a form of immunity. You can say whatever you want to say. You are protected, in a sense, when answering questions. Roughly speaking, this is the procedure we will be following. If you encounter any problems, please inform us of the fact. You will be testifying this morning, and you should be able to leave at the beginning of the afternoon. Without wasting any more time, I will now give the floor to Defence counsel who will start with their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ribo. Before -- I would first like to draw your attention to the following fact: We speak the same language, so when you hear my question you might want to answer it immediately, but it is particularly important for the Chamber and for all my colleagues in the courtroom to hear what is being said, and it is necessary for the interpreters to be able to interpret the questions and the answers. This is why when I have finished my question, I would be grateful if you could pause and then answer the question. Have you understood me?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've said where you were born and when. Tell me about your educational background, please.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I completed secondary school in Vitez and the Military Academy for the land forces from 1975 to 1979. This is a school I completed in Belgrade, and I specialised in Banja Luka, in the field of armed mechanised units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you live after you were born or, rather, up until the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I lived in the village of Kljaci, all the time. That's where I was born and after I went to the Military Academy, I no longer lived in the territory of Travnik municipality. It was only on the 30th of March, 1992, that I returned to live in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was your profession before the beginning of the war, and in what branch? In which service of the army were you engaged?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I was an active member of the military, a member of the former JNA. I was the commander of the Mechanised Brigade in the field of an armed mechanised units -- unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've already mentioned that you had the rank of captain first class. What rank do you hold today?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: The rank I have is that of a brigadier in the BH Federation army. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, at some point in time did you leave the JNA and, if so, could you please tell us briefly about the reasons for doing so.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I left the JNA on the 30th of March, 1992. I did so because the JNA was no longer a people's army. It became a national army or, rather, it became the Serbian army. There was, naturally, no room for me in such an army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go when you left the JNA?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: When I left the JNA -- well, before leaving it, I exchanged my flat with a Serb, someone in Zajecar. I gave him my flat in Zajecar and he gave me his flat in Travnik. This was on the 25th of February, 1992, 1992, when I returned with my family. And on that date, I arrived in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Travnik, did you notice how the events of 1991 in -- in the former Yugoslavia reflected on the situation in Travnik, had an effect on the situation in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Well, they had a significant effect. What happened in Slovenia had a significant effect. I'm referring to the war in Slovenia. And when the army moved from -- from Slovenia and Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, that also had an effect. That was characteristic of that period. Naturally there are many other events. For example, the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 6th of April, the referendum that was previously held, recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the European Union, and naturally there was the attack on Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the situation in Travnik, tell me, did you at any point in time join any military formations and, if so, tell me which formations you joined.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. I joined the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because the Presidency of declared that this was the only legitimate military force at the time, so naturally I joined the Territorial Defence. That was a patriotic act on my behalf.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, in response to a question put to you by the President of the Chamber, you said that you were chief of the Municipal Staff and later on the commander of the 301st Mechanised Brigade. Let's go back to 1992 in the municipality of Travnik. Could you tell us how power and positions were divided in the municipality of Travnik when you arrived there and assumed the duties of chief.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, naturally, because the two victorious parties in the elections at that time were the HDZ and the SDA, naturally. In accordance with the election results, certain positions were assigned bearing in mind the -- the percentage of votes gained. I know that the SDA was able to appoint the commander of the municipal defence staff, whereas the Croats had the possibility of appointing the chief or the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived there, what sort of equipment did the Municipal Staff have at its disposal? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, of course. At the time the Municipal Staff didn't have any equipment at its disposal. All we had as a staff were premises in which we were located. We didn't even have resources. We didn't even have food. We had to go to Hotel Orient in Travnik to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since we have already seen on the basis of the evidence to date that the Territorial Defence used to have equipment and weapons, tell me, where were those weapons when you arrived there, since the staff didn't have the use of weapons.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Well, I know that the JNA had been given the order to take all the weapons of the Territorial Defence, not only in the Central Bosnian area but in the Zenica region as well. So the Territorial Defence had to hand over its weapons to the JNA. These were weapons that the municipality and companies had paid for. They were in warehouses, and they were under the full control of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time while you were chief or, rather, the commander of the Municipal Staff, at any point in time was this equipment returned to you?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No, never, because the JNA, in the early morning in -- on one day in May, left the barracks and went to a nearby elevation called Vilenica, having previously blown up all the facilities. So we weren't able to obtain any of that equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my colleagues inform me that on page 11, page 8, a part of the answer was not recorded, namely when the witness said that these -- this equipment was located in the Slimena depot, Slimena barracks. So I would like this to be entered into the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry about this, Mr. Ribo. Sometimes we have to intervene and take care of the transcript. You have said that during the withdrawal of the JNA, the barracks was mined. What happened to the equipment, to the assets?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: A huge amount of equipment, the greatest part, if you want in percentage 80 per cent of it was destroyed in the explosion, whereas the part that wasn't destroyed was mainly ammunition and artillery shells for 105-millimetre guns.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: While you were commander, would you be able to tell us how many weapons did the Municipal Staff in Travnik have compared to establishment amount?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: As of the 24th of July, I had 5.100 troops, mainly volunteers. Out of those 5.100 troops, 50 or so per cent were mobilised on a voluntary basis from the municipality of Travnik, and we had between 1.000 and 1.200 barrels – or guns for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just said that you had about 5.000 troops, mainly volunteers. In what way were people mobilised at the time into the Territorial Defence and into what units exactly of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: This was the time of the first skirmishes that happened in Turbe, an area west of Travnik about 10 to 15 kilometres away from Travnik. At first in these skirmishes the Patriotic League, the Green Berets, and volunteers from villages offered resistance. At that point, the system of mobilisation had not been developed yet. So with the departure of Serbs from Travnik to territory held by Republika Srpska, the mobilisation system fell apart and there was simply nobody left to carry out mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, you just mentioned that the defence of Travnik, relying Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond on volunteers and MUP members, that is policemen, began on the defence lines of Turbe near Travnik. Tell me, while you discharged the duties of commander of the Municipal Staff, what was, generally speaking, the combat situation in the territory of your municipality?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: The situation in the territory of Travnik was extremely complex, primarily in terms of combat situation, because we had mainly established a defence geared to defend us from the Serb aggressor, because before we had managed to take certain key positions, elevations or features, the Yugoslav People's Army, together with the Republika Srpska and its reservists managed to capture key strategic features and thus made it impossible to improve our position. So we were handicapped. We were at a very disadvantageous position. We were forced to hold positions that a soldier would normally never take. This was aggravated by a huge amount of refugees, about 80.000 of them, flowing in for whom we had to provide transport to save them from the areas where they were at risk. We also had to organise food for the refugees and for troops. All of this made the situation in Travnik in 1992 very complex and very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time in Travnik, did civilian authorities function, and did they have any obligations or responsibilities towards the army?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. The civilian authorities were fully in operation. As for their competencies and responsibilities towards the army, they had two main responsibilities towards members of the Territorial Defence. One, logistical supply, logistical support; and two, mobilisation. I don't remember that they had any other tasks or responsibilities towards the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You as Staff Commander, were you a member of the War Presidency of the Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As -- let me rephrase this. In view of those responsibilities of civilian authorities that you mentioned, can you tell me, did you face a certain attitude on the part of political and civilian agencies that could affect your position as commander of the Municipal Staff?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Of course. I had enormous problems and experienced huge pressure on my staff because I did not belong to any party. Pressure was being put on my personnel officers to cleanse the staff from communists and former Partisans, and I personally was under pressure because I had never visited the quarters of any party, I had never contacted any party. And in 1992, except for the occasion when I was elected Joint Commander, I never even entered the building of the municipality -- of the Municipal Assembly of Travnik. I was completely dedicated solely to defence issues, and I had so many problems, that I had no time for political talks with party representatives, no time for political canvassing. And in that period, I didn't even visit my own family more than, let's say, five times, although they were only 300 metres away from the quarters of the staff. And in view of all this pressure, in early July I had already filed my request to the regional staff in Zenica to relieve me of my duties. I was probably not in their good books and they did not see me as politically reliable enough to lead the staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which units on the territory of the Municipal Staff of Territorial Defence were established at the time, namely during your tenure as commander?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Those were units of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence divided into detachments and area staffs. We had an area staff, border guard. We had an area staff of Kravlje, an area staff Travnik, area staff Krpeljici, area staff Han Bila, Mehuric, and Ljuta Greda, plus detachment 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, you mentioned the enormous pressure you experienced because of the problem of refugees fleeing areas held by Serb forces. Can you tell me, did it happen at any point that some units were formed out of the ranks of these persons, these refugees to be resubordinated to the Municipal Staff?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No, not a single unit -- not a single such unit was formed and resubordinated to the Municipal Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher now to show the witness now a set of documents, and at the same time I would like to have them submitted to the Trial Chamber, the registry, our learned friends from the Prosecution, to the accused, and our colleagues from the Defence team of Brigadier Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I show you this document, let me ask you, did at any time organised Krajina people come to Travnik, and what was their position?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact month, but the first Krajina battalion came from Croatia, from Zagreb or Rijeka, I don't know exactly. But since it had 520 troops armed with 250 automatic rifles, the most modern weapons at the time, and all of them were uniformed properly, I placed them at the barracks in Travnik after clearing it with the regional staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please now look at document number 3. It has a number 446 at the top. And document under number 4. Its number is 0457. Will you please look at this document, 446, dated 18 August 1992. Can you identify this document? Do you know it?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I am familiar with the document, but even then, back then when I received it, and now I see the same shortcomings because it speaks of the 3rd Corps, whereas the 3rd Corps had not even been envisaged to be established at the time. The time concerned here is August.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document speak of a unit being resubordinated? In other words, does this document mention precisely the units that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. That is that document referring to the 1st Krajina Battalion which came from Croatia with 520 troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at document number 4, then. Its number is 0457. Do you know this document, or do you know anything about its contents?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I know this document, yes, because it refers to the establishment of the first independent infantry battalion. We call it Siprazje Battalion, and at a certain point it found itself in the territory of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, Mr. Ribo, which units -- in fact, you've told us which units were under the Municipal Staff. Who was your superior at the time?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: At the time my superior command was the district staff, the district defence staff of Zenica. Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have told us about the general situation in Travnik, about numerous refugees. Would you tell us what kind of property did those refugees bring with them to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Well, they couldn't come. They couldn't carry anything except the most basic personal belongings, some clothing, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to move to a different topic with you. At Travnik at that time, did Croatian people report to the Territorial Defence at the time? Did they answer call-ups in their majority? And if not, do you know if they organised themselves differently?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Right at the outset, the Croatian people had a totally different approach. They organised themselves into the Croatian Defence Council, which was simultaneously a political and a military organisation. At the beginning of my tenure as commander and a bit later when I was chief of staff, I would see Croatian men wearing insignia of the Croatian army. But later, a decision was obviously passed that these troops who had come from battlefields in Croatia, with experience and good equipment, should be renamed HVO. That was widely publicised and covered on television, in the media, analogously to what was going on in the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How did you as Staff Commander view the fact that a new armed force, much better equipped than yours, was suddenly appearing in your town?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Let me tell you, it was a very unpleasant situation. We expected and made some assessments to the effect that under joint command we would fight together against the Serb aggressor whom we saw as the only threat at the time. And the appearance of those armed units called HVO did not come as a surprise to me. We expected it in a way because we seemed to act on parallel tracks. We seemed to be doing the same things separately. So there was some indignation among the Bosniak population, and I personally had a multi-ethnic staff. There were both Muslims and Croats on the staff. And we were not hung up on the same things that they were, namely they -- we did not insist on creating a monoethnic army, unlike them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, did you as a commander attempt to resolve this situation? What steps did you take and what success did you have?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: It was more the politicians who took some steps. One day we were all invited into the Municipal Assembly to discuss the possibility of creating a joint command. I remember clearly that I was elected at that meeting joint commander of the armed defence forces of Travnik. However, after lip-service was paid to that commitment and after general applause and after the Croatian agreement to my appointment as joint commander, I never actually managed to establish overall command over the joint forces of the Territorial Defence and the HVO. I did not succeed for many reasons. I met the HVO commander several times, but they wanted to have everything of their own in parallel. They did not really want a joint structure. In those negotiations, they insisted mainly on one thing. They wanted our sparse equipment and resources to be placed from our depots into one joint depot. And after my refusal, I thought again and realised that I did well to refuse, because if I had agreed, we, the Territorial Defence, would have been left stranded without a single round or shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to this lack of willingness to place themselves under joint command on their part, were there any incidents or skirmishes, minor or major, between the TO and HVO units?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Let me tell you, there were no major incidents, but there was certainly problems that made our life very difficult, especially my life as commander. First of all, my staff headquarters is no bigger than this room, which was an abandoned restaurant. At a certain point, they started taking over one after another building in town. And the people of Travnik came to me and sometimes threatened: Either we go to Hotel Orient and retake it from them or I don't know what. And I would try to calm them down and tell them, "We can recapture the hotel and even destroy it now, but our main objective is preserve peace." Because that is a very important building in Travnik. Everyone who came to Travnik used it. We had huge problems with routes that went through Croatian villages, especially with Dzelilovac village. We had to send troops to the mount Sesic and some other positions, and these troops had to pass through this village, and they would be disarmed there. We had to go defuse tensions, demand our weapons back, et cetera. They had also set up a vast amount of checkpoints. Whenever they saw their interest in putting a checkpoint somewhere they would do so without our agreement or approval. Once when I was going to the superior command in Zenica, the police force of Mr. Blaskic disarmed me at the intersection in Vitez on the road towards Vjetrenica, but I also took some steps, and I threatened that I would arrest Blaskic in Travnik the next time you comes, because he had to come to Travnik occasionally. And I cannot remember all the things I said, but I demanded very firmly that my weapons be given back to me, because it was an insult to my dignity. I had never attempted to do something like that to them. My units never did such things to them. So I was very hurt by this indeed. When I told you at one point that there was no one left to carry out mobilisation, I can also add that the secretary of the national defence secretariat in Travnik was unable to discharge his normal regular duties because he was busy stopping me at a checkpoint in Guca Gora. He personally set up this checkpoint near his home. And when I had to pass by his house, that man stopped me on the road. Instead of busying himself with what was actually his job, dealing with mobilisation issues, he was manning this checkpoint of his.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at document under number 1, 410 is the number of the document; and document under number 5, 486; under number 7, 489, 5, 6, and 7, and 8. Document number 8 too. Document number 1 and then 5, 6, 7, and 8. Have a look at those documents. I will then ask you a couple of questions about them. These are HVO documents. Mr. Ribo, when you have a look at the contents of these documents, would you say that these documents refer to certain situations and events, the manner in which the HVO behaved and to events that you experienced in Travnik in 1992.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I haven't seen such documents before. I didn't have access to such documents. These are HVO documents. But when I see these documents, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond it's quite clear to me that they reflect the situation in accordance with their orders. The most important thing for them was to set up checkpoints. If you talked about a problem with them, they would say they didn't have the authority to negotiate. They would say they were waiting for the green light from a higher level, et cetera, et cetera. And on the other page -- and on the other side, on the other hand, they acted contrary to what was said, contrary to what had been agreed. So these documents reflect the situation on our roads with respect to controlling communications, roads, movement, et cetera. There was -- people were humiliated, et cetera. These were all things that I experienced.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ribo, could we now move on to another subject. As commander of the Municipal Staff and at that time as a citizen of Travnik, because if I've understood you well you didn't live in Travnik earlier on, but on the -- upon returning from the JNA, as a citizen of Travnik and as commander of the Municipal Staff, did you notice that at some point in time in 1992 foreigners started arriving in Travnik, foreigners who weren't from the area of the former Yugoslavia, nor were they members of one of the peoples from the are of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: There were a lot of foreigners who passed through. In my staff I even had a commander who was a foreigner. Mihajlo Petrovic was from Belgrade, a Serb. He was a commander of the Lasic detachment. His deputy was a Slovenia, and all the other combatants in the detachment were Muslims. There were UNPROFOR representatives. I personally spoke to the first commander of BritBat. Bob Stewart was his name. There were journalists who passed through, for example, Guardian journalists. There were representatives of humanitarian organisations. There were many such foreigners who were there for various reasons. There were journalists from foreign countries, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to those foreigners whom you saw -- well, first tell me, what was the main reason for which those foreigners, the journalists and the representatives of humanitarian organisations, what was the main reason for them going to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Well, my opinion is that they came because we would send a lot of information to -- abroad from Travnik. Not via the Bosnian television or Sarajevo television, but we would send our footage to Split, the vehicles which would go to Split so that they could inform others of the catastrophe in Travnik. There were thousands of refugees in Travnik. It was impossible to know how to find accommodation for them. There were people who were barefoot in the street. They were hungry. They would turn to you to ask you to bury their child who had died in one of the extremely arduous transports, et cetera. So probably because of information that we sent abroad, the first kind of information we sent was that the Serbs were firing on us with a surface-to-surface missiles. There was a projectile that fell near the church and near a settlement near the Vilenica mountain. So we were the first to shoot such events, to make footage of such event and inform the world of such events, to depict the humanitarian catastrophe. I won't even mention the fall of Jajce and the fact that the population of one town moved towards Karaula, and they were all within the range of fire of Serbian soldiers. The valley was such that this was possible. Or you would have a trailer lorry full of children and old people. It would then be -- there would then be an accident. There would be lots of dead people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you have provided a very clear description of the foreigners who would come to Travnik and of people who would come to Travnik. Tell me, in addition to those humanitarian organisations and journalists from the West, did you notice that there were individuals coming from African or Asian countries or perhaps from Arab countries? Did you notice the presence of such people, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I spoke to and met people who would come to my staff. I can't say anything about others. I can only talk about those with whom I spoke in my staff. On one day, 40 journalists from Egypt appeared. They came, they discussed the situation with me, and they wanted me to make a list of what we needed for defence. I provided them with that list, and when they saw it, they left, and I never saw those people again. Then on one day, ten journalists from Turkey appeared, and there were people with them who a hundred years ago were in the same condition as Bosnians who had left Krajina. People came with them who had gone to Turkey in similar conditions. I know that they met with the command of the Patriotic League in Gluha Bukovica because they wanted me to be present there. I know on that occasion they gave him 40.000 German Marks to help with the resistance, to obtain weapons, et cetera. A humanitarian organisation based here in the Netherlands also appeared on one occasion. They came to ask us what we needed. On that occasion they gave us about 12.000 marks, and they then left, and I never saw those people again. So these are the kind of people who would appear. For example, there was the Guardian journalist who left with the refugees from Banja Luka. He appeared in my staff, asked me to help him. I provided him with accommodation and food and gave him a vehicle to take him to Split so that he could return home because the Serbs had confiscated his vehicle just before he entered the zone which we controlled, just before he passed through the lines and entered the zone under our control.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I've been informed that on page 23, line 24, there is a mistake. The witness said that this money, these thousands of marks, I don't know what the amount is, was given to the Patriotic League, and as far as I say, it appears -- it seems that that money was given to the witness, but you can see from the transcript that the witness was present at the meeting. That's why he was aware of this fact. Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I was called to witness that. The money wasn't for me or the Municipal Staff. It was for the Patriotic League which was from Zenica, which was holding my right wing of defence. The man who was the commander of the Patriotic League asked me to come and witness the fact that they handed over that money to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1992, did you witness the arrival of armed individuals in Travnik, individuals who were from African or Arab countries, and did such people ever go to the Municipal Staff of the Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Such armed individuals never appeared. I didn't notice them. They never came to the municipal or Territorial Defence Staff in particular.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the Municipal Territorial Defence Staff, while you were its commander, in any way plan any action with those foreigners, and did the Municipal Staff ever provide logistical support for foreigners who might have been present in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: First of all, I never saw such people in the staff. I never spoke to them. And while I was the commander, I didn't participate in any defence activities at the defence lines, which were 60 kilometres long in mountainous terrain. And similarly, there's an order of mine stating that all those who weren't part of the Territorial Defence had nothing to do in the Territorial Defence Staff. Nor could they be provided with logistical support on any grounds. So this was what was said at a briefing in my staff when I assigned tasks to all unit commanders. So while I was present there, none of their soldiers participated in action, nor was logistical support provided to any of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, where was the command of your Mehurici detachment located?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: The command of the Mehurici detachment was located in the Mehurici primary school, on the ground floor, and this included a number of classrooms, the common room which was used by the teachers, and the kitchen, the school kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, who requisitioned facilities and buildings for the needs of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: This was done and had to be done through the Secretariat for National Defence in Travnik municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, in the early autumn of 1992, did you visit your detachment in Mehurici, and if so, did you find any other individuals there, apart from members of your detachment?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. I would visit the detachments. I would visit their commands and their defence lines as well, and I don't know whether that was towards the end of August or the beginning of September, but I had a meeting in Mehurici with my detachment. And then at that time while I was in Mehurici, we also discussed certain Muslim forces, and the detachment commander mentioned this was a problem. And during that visit, I didn't notice any foreigners in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, while you were commander, did anyone inform you that some foreigners wanted to find accommodation in some military facilities in the area of Travnik? And if you were informed of this, could you elaborate on it?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Some civilians came to see me, and they said that for the needs of foreign humanitarian organisations, I should provide the Slimena barracks which had been completely destroyed. But since I was responsible for buildings of the former JNA, for example, the Travnik barracks or the Slimena barracks, I didn't allow this for security reasons, above all, because this was a mined area. And after the explosions, there were 18 seriously wounded individuals. They'd lost limbs. Some had died in minefields around those barracks. So this was for security reasons. Secondly, I couldn't provide a military facility for humanitarian organisation. I didn't have this right. And thirdly, when I asked who was concerned, I was told it was some sort of Arab humanitarian organisation and I said that's out of the question because the population was mixed, and I didn't want to provoke incidents or cause problems. I tried to calm the situation down in an appropriate way, which is what a commander should do. And I said that the population there was mixed, and if there was an Arab humanitarian organisation there, that would cause problems. I said it wasn't good, and they shouldn't insist on this. I rejected this idea immediately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, you mentioned the Muslim forces awhile ago. Tell me, did you ever take a decision on forming Muslim forces in Travnik, or did you perhaps hear about the formation of such forces in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: To answer your first question, the first part of your question, no, I never issued an order or document, nor did my superior command take any decision on the formation of Muslim forces of any kind, on the formation of any forces other than the Territorial Defence. That was the only legitimate force. So no official decisions or documents were made.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As commander of the Municipal Staff, did you find out that in Travnik, towards the end of the summer or the beginning of the autumn, such forces were being formed?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. If I had an assistant commander for security who didn't know what was happening in the situation in the field, that would be difficult to understand. So the assistant for security in my staff provided information according to which they were preparing to form certain Muslim forces. I was especially angry about this, and members of the command were, too, because I had Serbs and Croats in the command, and I reacted by trying to find out who was forming those forces and to find out who these people were, to find out where they were from and to find out who appointed their commander. I wanted to know what they wanted. This was a problem for me as a commander, because we were living in very difficult conditions and fighting in very difficult conditions, and then you find yourself in a situation which another force is being formed, and this causes problems. We had various forces. We had forces from the Krajina. We had the HVO. We had the HOS. There were the Handzar units. There were units come from neighbouring municipalities, from Vitez, from Travnik, or, rather, from Novi Travnik, from Zenica. They came to assist me. I informed the Municipal Staff of the information my security organs had provided me with. I informed them of what was happening in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who commanded those forces when they were formed, and when were they formed?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I knew that a certain Asim Koricic was the commander of those forces, a man outside the territory of Travnik, outside of Central Bosnia, for that matter. Later on, I learned that he was a native of Krajina. He may have come together with the refugees. In any case, he was the first commander of those Muslim armed forces that I learned about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it was not you who established those forces. Did you disband them, and do you know what happened to them later? But before you tell us Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond this, tell us first who was in those units? Because you had made your inquiries.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Most of those troops of those units were refugees from Jajce, from Bosnian Krajina, some from Travnik itself, especially young, inexperienced people, not warriors at all. At that time, it seemed to be only important to form the unit regardless of who's going to be in it. And as I had no say in establishing it, I had no say in disbanding it. Since I personally stayed on in the 3rd Corps, I know that they were disbanded in Travnik, and they were added to the 1st Battalion of the 7th Mechanised Brigade. Some of them went to their original units which were then located in Travnik, whereas yet another part started wandering about. I think these people were actually fakes, because what they really wanted was to keep living in those buildings where they held their religious rights and to receive humanitarian aid in money and food, something that our troops did not enjoy. Our troops had a salary of four Deutschmarks and had nothing to feed their families with.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Ribo. You said you worked 20 hours a day. You described the situation as very dramatic. Let me ask you, did all this effort that you had to invest take a toll on your health eventually, and did you have to leave your job for a while as a result?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: It's not that I worked 20 hours a day. I was constantly in my workplace. I didn't leave the staff quarters. I slept on chairs. We had no decent accommodation. What I literally did was to put three chairs to the and take a nap for an hour or two at a time. We had a difficult situation when Karaula fell. It was captured by the Serb-Montenegrin aggressor. And all these problems were problems I had to deal with. Young men were dying. I had to tell their mothers, their families. There were many families that had to be taken care of. Very seriously wounded men sometimes needed to be send abroad for proper treatment. And there was a point, I believe it was towards the end of my tenure in Travnik, I had to be transported to Travnik, to the hospital where I needed a drip, and I eventually received orders from my superior commander, Sefer Halilovic to transfer to Zenica and to establish the 301st Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have about ten questions left for this witness, and since this seems to be the right time for the break, I suggest that we take the break now maybe and finish after. I think I need only about ten more minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will continue about five to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Before I continue the question of the witness, I would only like it on record that on page 29, line 25, which reads, "I didn't work 20 hours a day," the witness actually said he worked much more, and he was constantly in his workplace, and that bit where he actually specified how much he worked is not recorded. We can go through it again with the witness, but that's what I heard him saying originally. And on page 30, lines 10 to 12, it says the witness was ill and that he had an intravenous drip. The witness, in addition to that, said that he had heart trouble, maybe a heart attack even. The witness can specify, but that bit again is not recorded in the transcript. So I will ask the witness again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What were the health problems that resulted in your hospitalisation and the intravenous drip?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I was experiencing heart trouble at the moment, heart problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would now like to ask you, Mr. Ribo, was there a time in end 1992 when organisational changes occurred in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? If you know, tell us what kind of changes, and what position did you occupy afterwards?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I know that organisational changes occurred toward the end of 1992. Units became larger. In fact, units merged. Brigades and the corps were established. And according to the order from the Supreme Command, I came to Zenica and took over the command of the 301st Mechanised Brigade, which I knew had been established.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Please look at document under number 2 now. Rules of service in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Tell me, Mr. Ribo, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: It certainly is, because from the very beginning, we insisted that this kind of regulation be adopted as soon as possible so that the troops would have a soldierly appearance and manner and act according to regulations in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at page 391. It deals with the issue of accommodation and work. Tell me, please, was there any time in 1992 when you were commander of the Municipal Staff and later in 1993 when you were brigade commander that you had barracks and the terms and conditions envisaged by this regulation for your troops?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No. I mean to say that we had no proper facilities for accommodating our personnel. And in 1992, this 1st Krajina Battalion which was accommodated in the Travnik barracks went straight from defence lines on leave to their homes and back on the front line. So for the most part, our units did not have, in 1992 or even 1993, facilities for proper permanent accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were your weapons deposited?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: All our weaponry was on our defence lines, which means that we did not have the possibility to deposit our weapons at the barracks or at the depot. The weapons would change hands when shifts changed. The personnel on the defence line would turn over their weapons and positions together to the new shift who came to replace them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Despite that, did you in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina attempt to turn such troops into real soldiers, to introduce discipline, and how successful were you in these efforts in 1992 and in 1993?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Of course every soldier thrives on proper order and discipline in the army, and that is why we took certain steps to build, consciously, discipline among the troops, to promote proper conduct in keeping with the regulations. And of course there were certain problems in command and control. What do I mean? I mean that in 1992 or throughout that year Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond practically we didn't have any volunteers. And the greatest problem with that is sometimes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: We had to rely on volunteers throughout 1992,.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the greatest problem was that when you gave them an order to take up positions on defence line they would sometimes refuse or if they would go they would on their own leave positions or if they would hear somebody was ill at home or they had a family problem. For instance, once on Mount Sesic in the unit of Commander Mesanovic, we didn't manage to supply bread in time and the complete unit threatened to leave their position. In another situation, they asked 25 kilos of flour to be supplied to their families, and they threatened to leave their position its if we didn't do that. So we had all kinds of problems. They would take food from the canteens that belonged to specific enterprises for the personnel of these enterprises exclusively. It was very hard to establish proper order and discipline, because we did not have proper army personnel with superior officers who were qualified and trained, commanders of brigades, commanders of subordinate units, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you another thing. As the commander -- as an officer in the BH army, who did you have command over?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: As commander of the Municipal Staff, I only had command over the members of my own unit, nobody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that while you were in the hospital, you assumed the duty of the command of the 301st Mechanised Brigade. Through these attempts to organise yourself and the circumstances under which you had to operate, that up until the end of 1993, were you able to carry out the order? Were you able to form the 301st Mechanised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: My answer is no, certainly not. Up until the end of 1993, I wasn't able to form the brigade. I formed one battalion within that brigade, one armoured battalion, and one mechanised battalion. But because I wasn't able to carry out the work completely for various reasons, because we didn't have sufficient materiel and equipment, for this reason this brigade was disbanded in November 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness kindly slow down a little, please, when he answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So in spite of all these efforts, you weren't able to form that brigade. Do you know whether similar difficulties were encountered by other 3rd Corps units of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Well, I can say that that's indisputable. There were problems in all units, and none of the brigade commanders ever managed to complete the formation of his brigade. This never happened. We had an order according to which a sabotage unit in Zenica was to be formed. A commander was appointed, and some members of the command were appointed, but this soon came to nothing. This was the case in all units, not just in my brigade. It was the case in all brigades. It was not possible to carry through the work because of insufficient equipment, because of inadequate manpower. It wasn't possible to form complete brigades in accordance with the relevant establishment for our brigades, for battalions, and for other units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't form it, but did you take any measures? Was there anything else you could have done up until the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I did everything I could. There was nothing else that I as brigade commander could have done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, when you compare this mechanised battalion that you formed at the end of 1993, when you compare it with the mechanised battalion or a mechanised battalion in the JNA in which you were a commander, would you say that there were any differences between the two, and what were the differences?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. Naturally there were differences. The differences were enormous. At the beginning of the war, professional members of the former JNA had problems with our subordinates for this very reason, because when we assigned them units, they thought that I as commander of the Municipal Staff had the warehouses of the former JNA where ammunition for tanks, ammunition for artillery, fuel, lorries, tents, et cetera. So they were confused. They even asked, the Mehurici detachment asked for enormous tents for accommodation. I told them where am I supposed to find such tents? The differences were enormous because in these tanks I had 25 litres of fuel when we were to carry out a task. And that's sufficient for one T-55 tank to work for one hour. So in the former JNA we had a tank of fuel that would provide fuel for the tanks. The tanks were always full. They had sufficient fuel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you have answered all my questions, Mr. Ribo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have now finished with my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have taken up an hour and a half, which is what had been planned. Are there any questions for this witness from the other Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We would just like to ask this witness a few questions in order to clarify some of his answers provided in the course of the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ribo, in response to a question from my colleague Mrs. Residovic, you mentioned the Muslim forces. I think it's on page 28 and on page 29 of the transcript. If I have understood you well, you said that these Muslim forces were mainly composed of refugees from Bosanska Krajina, from Jajce. They were composed of refugees, et cetera; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. On the whole they were composed of men from those areas, but there were also men from Travnik municipality, and I did emphasise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that these Muslim forces were composed of men and young men who were Bosnians, and there were no foreigners in these forces?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: As far as I know, that was the case. I never inspected that formation. As far as I know, it was composed only of citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When these Muslim forces ceased to exist, that's when organisational changes were made in the BH army. That was October, Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond November, December 1992. You said that at that time some of the members of the Muslim forces joined the Travnik Battalion of the 7th Brigade, and others joined the mother units. Would the mother unit be the 306th Brigade from Travnik, the 312th Brigade, and the 17th Krajina Brigade from Travnik. Are those the units concerned?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, you are completely right. Some of them became part of the 1st Battalion of the 7th, which was part of the 3rd Corps of the BH army. Some of them remained within the 306th, and the 312th, and some of them became part of the 17th Krajina Brigade. Naturally these people made calculations, because this battalion became part of the 7th with its headquarters in Zenica. So that would mean leaving the Travnik municipality, and as a result they preferred to remain in their territory, in the territory of their municipalities. So this was the calculation that is some of the men made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, you may take the floor for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. My name is Daryl Mundis, and I represent the Prosecution in this case. I'm going to be asking you some questions that will probably take a little bit more than an hour. Before I do that, I simply want to make sure that you understand that I'm not in any way trying to trick you or put words in your mouth. If I ask any questions that you don't understand, I would like you to simply tell me that and I will rephrase the question. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to start off by talking a little bit about - excuse me - a little bit about the Muslim forces or the Muslimanske Snage that you've talked about earlier this morning. You told us that when you became aware of the formation of that unit that you became upset and asked the -- your security chief to find out who these people were. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: That's not right. I had information provided to me by my chief of security, who is a subordinate of mine in the staff. He said that he had information according to which some sort of preparations were underway for formation of Muslim armed forces. So this was previous information. This information had been obtained prior to the establishment of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when it was that your chief of security informed you or provided you with this information? Do you recall the approximate month or day, year?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Perhaps it was in July. I can't provide you with the precise answer to that question. I have documents of my own in which this has been recorded, but I can't remember now. I believe that it was in June or July. Either in June or July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again for the benefit of the transcript, that would be 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, of course, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you've just mentioned that you have some documents of your own in which this might be recorded. Did you happen to bring these documents with you to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No, I haven't brought them with me, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on the information that was provided to you by your chief of security, what steps, if any, did you take or order the security chief to take with respect to determining who these people were and what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Well, I remember that at one meeting I instructed my chief or, rather, assistant commander for security to see which forces were concerned and to find out who their commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can I just ask you at this point, sir, the name of your assistant commander for security at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: His name was Esad Sipic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what information Esad Sipic provided to you after you tasked him with determining who these forces were and who their commander was?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Esad Sipic provided me with information. Well, first I had requested information about the commander whose name was apparently Major Tara. I don't know who this person was. He suddenly appeared in that area, and I was informed of the identity of this person, Major Tara, and the assistant commander for security also -- he provide immediate with this information, and I relayed that information to the deputy commander for security in the district. I think his name was Mr. Agic. So I forwarded this information to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the period of June and July 1992, other than what you've told us now, did you obtain any other information about the Muslimanske Snage?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No, I didn't obtain any other information. I don't remember receiving any other information. Perhaps I did. But this was an insignificant unit in my opinion, so I didn't pay much attention to it. I had so many problems of my own that it just did not concern me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The person that you -- the name you've given us, Major -- can you spell the name of that individual if you know?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Major Tara. The assistant for security found out that his name was Redzic, Emir. Redzic Emir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And is the name Major Dara with a "d," or Tara with a "t"?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: With a T.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let us move into later 1992 and into the autumn of 1992. During that time period while you remained the commander of the Travnik municipal TO, did you obtain any other information about the Muslimanske Snage?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: If you're referring to the Muslim forces from Travnik, no. I didn't obtain any other information because I wasn't particularly interested in them, to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, if I understood what you said correctly earlier, and I believe this is page 28, line 19, you also mentioned in connection with the Muslim forces the name Asim Koricic. Did you tell the Trial Chamber that Asim Koricic was a commander of the Muslim forces in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. He was the first commander. He was called commander, but I'm not sure whether he really was a commander, but that's what he was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this Major Tara, what position did he hold within the Muslim forces in Travnik? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: He took over from Commander Asim Koricic. Major Tara took over from Asim Koricic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate time period that Major Tara took over from Asim Koricic?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what Asim Koricic did following the time period he commanded the Muslim forces in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I don't know, because I had already left Travnik. So I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: From mid-November 1992 through I believe you've said November 1993, you were the commander of the 301st Mechanised Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. From the 20th of November, 1992, until the 30th of November, 1993, I was the commander of the Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the time period that you were the commander of the 301st Mechanised Brigade, on how many occasions did you have meetings with the leadership of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say, but I would estimate we had a meeting every month. But if there were any extraordinary situations, then these meetings would be held more frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your answer, sir, would it then be correct that you would have attended more than 12 such meetings during the time that you were the commander of the 301st?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether we could say more than 12. Perhaps more, perhaps less. I couldn't give you a precise answer. I didn't make a record of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At these meetings with the 3rd Corps Command, were other brigade commanders also present?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: These meetings were only attended by establishment commanders who were part of the 3rd Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would the subordinate brigades of the 3rd Corps Command be included within the term "establishment commanders"?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I haven't answered your question. Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Certainly. I asked you two questions ago if brigade commanders were also present at the 3rd Corps meetings, and you told us these meetings were only attended by establishment commanders who were part of the 3rd Corps Command. My follow-up question is: When you say "establishment commanders who were part of the 3rd Corps Command," do you mean commanders of the brigades that were part of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I'm referring exclusively to the brigade commanders that were part of the 3rd Corps, but in certain situations individual brigade commanders, because of problems in the units or because of the situation in the battlefield, they were not able to attend the regular meetings. They would remain in their units, and the corps command would provide them authorisation to do this. So in certain cases, not all the brigade commanders would be present at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know or do you recall if at any of the 3rd Corps meetings attended by brigade commanders Asim Koricic attended as the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I can't remember, to be frank. I don't even know when he became brigade commander. But I do know that the brigade commander of the 7th Mechanised -- of the 7th Muslim attended these meeting or was present when tasks were being assigned, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And who was the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade who attended these 3rd Corps meetings?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I can remember Asim Koricic. I can remember Kubura. I can remember -- there were two other commanders after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I think there was General Brsine and one other commander whose name I can't remember right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused, sir, because of a couple of the answers you've given, so I'd like to try to clear this up. Do you remember the time period in which Asim Koricic attended 3rd Corps meetings as the commander of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Well, it's very difficult for me to answer that question, because afterwards, in -- I continued to be a member of the corps command up until the end of the war. So a lot of these commanders changed, and I wasn't just paying attention to the commanders of the 7th. Many commanders in other brigades were changed. So it's difficult for me to say exactly when Asim Koricic was the commander since after my duties as a brigade commander, I became a member of the 3rd Corps Command right up until the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question, and again if you don't recall, that's fine. In 1993, do you recall the last time you saw Asim Koricic?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No. No, I can't remember that at all .

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on to a different, slightly different topic. I believe you told us in response to some questions concerning foreign Arab or Middle Eastern fighters that you never met with such persons at the headquarters of the Territorial Defence in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we just correct something in the transcript? Line 44. Line to the witness in fact said that he became a member of the 3rd Corps Command and was a member of the 3rd Corps Command right up until the end of 1996, whereas the transcript says up until the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I thank my learned colleague for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me return to the question, sir. Do you remember saying earlier this morning, I believe it's page 25, line 3, that you never saw any armed Arab or Middle Eastern fighters at your TO headquarters in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: That's correct. No such individuals appeared. No such armed individuals appeared either. These individuals weren't in uniform. They wore traditional clothes. So they didn't come to see me for any reasons. They didn't come in uniform or carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did you meet with these or have any contact with these individuals in any other locations? You said they didn't come to the TO. Did you have any meetings or contacts with these people anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No, I had no meetings with them. And we were great opponents, in fact. I was not able to communicate with then, and I didn't want any meetings with them. I'm talking about 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's fine. That's what I'm talking about as well, the period Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond when you were the commander of the TO in Travnik. Are you telling us, sir, that you had no contacts at any time with any Mujahedin in -- anywhere?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No. No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You were aware, however, that persons who would fall within the term "foreign Mujahedin" were present in Travnik, Travnik municipality during this time period?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe it is the term used here in the Tribunal or maybe in the OTP. Maybe you call them Mujahedin. We used derogatory terms for them such as Mudzos, but we used the same term for people who wore long beards and even members of the Muslim armed forces were called Mudzos. I'm not familiar with this term Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. And just so we're clear, can you describe for us when you use the term "Mudzos" who you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I mean members of the Muslim armed forces, because they cultivated this appearance with beards, et cetera. So we called them Mudzos. In 1992 when I was commander, this term "Mujahedin" was not a familiar one. I learned of it only later, maybe in 1993, or 1994 even.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
