utterances.text: Let me ask you a follow-up question. You defined these people as members of the Muslim armed forces. They cultivated this appearance with beards. Were the people that you called or referred to as Mudzos local Bosniaks or foreigners or both or neither?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Those were only Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me focus, then, your attention on foreign-born fighters. Are you aware of the presence, during the period from June through November 1992 when you were the Travnik TO commander, of foreign-born fighters present in Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you become aware of such persons?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: That was the Croatian army. It passed through with two M-47 tanks that were on their way to Jajce. They were foreign-born fighters with clearly visible emblems, clearly visible to everybody who followed them on the route from Gornji Vakuf to Jajce. They clearly wore emblems of the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll get to the Croatian army later this morning. I want to ask you about persons from the Middle East, persons from North Africa, and persons from the continent of Asia. Were you aware of any of these persons being present in the Travnik municipality from June through November of 1992? And I mean these persons being armed fighters, not humanitarian workers, not members of BritBat, not members of UNPROFOR, and not members of the Croatian army, the HOS, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I am not aware that such persons were there. I'm not aware of the presence of such troops.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. In October of 1992, while you were the commander of the TO in Travnik, were you aware of allegations or rumours that the leader of the Arab Mujahedin in Bosnia had been captured by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm hearing about this, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the month of October 1992, then, I assume that you will say that you were not contacted by any newspapers from London asking you about the capture of an Arab Mujahedin leader by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I never had such a contact with any journalist, any reporter, or anyone else. I never had such a discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about an individual by the name of Abu Abdel Aziz. Have you ever heard the name "Abu Abdel Aziz"?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I heard of that name. I heard of the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When, to the best of your recollection, did you first hear that name?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly, but I think it could have been perhaps towards the end of 1993, because I really had no communication with those people. I just heard from some fellow townsfolk. They were talking about some Sheik Abu Abdel Aziz, but I can't remember in which period I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier, sir, a journalist from the Guardian newspaper. Was that Ed Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No. First of all, I didn't mention the name of the journalist, and to this day I haven't learnt his name. All I know is that he was a journalist writing from the -- for the Guardian. He asked me to borrow my vehicle to go back to his press house because the Serbs had seized his vehicle on Mount Vlasic. But there is a book that this journalist wrote about the expulsion of Bosniaks from the Bosnian Krajina, and there is a reference to my name in that book and some of the things I have mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a different journalist. Do you recall at any point in time in 1992 meeting or speaking on the telephone with or having any contact with an individual named Andrew Hogg of the Sunday Times of London?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I never spoke to that journalist, not even on the phone. The only two Englishmen who came to my command headquarters while I was commander were the commander of the SFOR and this journalist from the Guardian. I never spoke to this other person, nor did I give him any statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall at any point in time from June through November 1992 whether any journalist sought your assistance in finding the location of any of the foreign-born fighters who were present in Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No, never. Not then and not later. I didn't talk to that man. He didn't call me. Quite simply, I didn't have any contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Before I move on to a different topic, I just have a couple of final questions on this subject. You told us that you were not aware of any foreign-born fighters present in Travnik municipality from June through November 1992. I take it then, sir, you didn't see any such people.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: That's correct, because I spent very, very little time outside the staff headquarters. I just told the Defence counsel in response to her question that I spent 24 hours a day at the staff headquarters. There was a canteen there where I took my meals. I barely ever went to see my family once a month, even though they were only 300 metres away from the staff headquarters. So I didn't see any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you -- did you receive any reports from any of your subordinates, including your chief of security, Esad Sipic, to the effect that such foreign-born fighters were present in Travnik municipality during the period June through November 1992? Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me move on -- well, let me ask you a different question. Do you know Jozo Pokrajcic?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm probably botching the name. Family name is P-o-k-r-a-j-c-i-c, first name Jozo?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No. No. I don't know that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know a person with a similar name who was the HVO commander in Travnik in 1992, 1993?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: No, no one with a name like that. No one of that or similar name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me return, then, to the subject that you mentioned just a few moments ago, and that was the Croatian army. What can you tell us about the presence of the Croatian army, as you put it, in the period 1992 and 1993 in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: What I know from the time when I was commander of Municipal Staff is all I know about it, because later on when I moved to Zenica to assume another position I was no longer in Travnik. But what I know from that time, Croatian troops wore HV emblems. Croatian army, HV. And as I said before, two tanks, M-47, passed through on their way to Jajce. They also wore Croatian army signs and emblems. And there were some soldiers accompanying the tank, not on the tank but on foot. I don't know whose units these two tanks belonged to, but I also know that HOS forces, Croatian Armed Forces, were also present in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, whether the HV, that is the army of the Republic of Croatia, was supplying manpower to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object, since the previous questions and those before it have nothing to do with examination-in-chief or the subject of the indictment. I don't think they are relevant, and I don't think they should continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you respond to this objection, Mr. Mundis, based on the fact that the examination-in-chief did not refer to the Croatian army, the HV? And secondly, the question of the Croatian army presence does not feature in the indictment. And the Defence is asking why you are pursuing this line of questioning and what is the relevance to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, you will -- you will recall -- actually, if I could do this in the absence of the witness, I would greatly appreciate that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We will lose another couple of minutes then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Chamber will be aware that in response to a question about the presence of foreigners, this witness answered that he was certainly aware that there were foreign fighters and they came from Croatia. The Prosecution would like to explore this a bit further with this witness. This witness has previously provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor with respect to a different case and in a different investigation. In his statement, he provides a number of details concerning the presence of forces and military equipment from the Republic of Croatia present during the indictment period in this conflict that was between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslim forces or the ABiH. Moreover, Mr. President, as the Chamber is well aware, the Prosecution throughout the course of its case consistently, in the early phases, objected to the Defence position with respect to contextual evidence. The Chamber's rulings are quite clear that the Defence is entitled to provide a very broad political, military, and historical context in which these crimes or alleged crimes in our indictment occurred. The Prosecution, although we, with all due respect, don't believe that this broad contextual approach is merited in this case, will certainly -- we have certainly respected the Chamber's rulings in this respect. It seems to us, however, that by putting on a defence that brings in the broadest possible context in which the crimes were allegedly committed would certainly include, for the sake of completeness, any evidence to the effect that the Republic of Croatia may have been involved even in a limited way in this conflict. And it is our position that when witnesses such as the present one, we believe, have information or are witnesses to events concerning the presence of forces, equipment, or manpower of the Republic of Croatia that we should be allowed to put that information before the Trial Chamber, again so that Your Honours have the broadest possible understanding of the context in which this -- the alleged crimes in our indictment occurred. This was not the initial approach to be taken by the Prosecution. However, in light of the Trial Chamber's rulings during the initial phases of the Prosecution's case and in light of the fact that this witness apparently has some of these events, we respectfully suggest that this line of questioning, and it's not -- it won't take very long, should be allowed so that you -- that Your Honours have the fullest possible picture of the entire context in which the alleged crimes occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will give the floor again to the Defence, but I would like to summarise two pages of the transcript. The Prosecution tells us that on a particular issue the witness himself said there had been foreigners, and he said, yes, there was the Croatian army, the present of the Croatian army. So it was the witness himself who referred, who brought up the Croatian army. He described two tanks with insignia of the Croatian army. Proceeding from there, the Prosecution tells us that they are in possession of a written statement of this witness that the Trial Chamber does not have before it but which the Defence certainly is entitled to see, because it comes from another case but it should have been supplied by the Defence. And in this statement, the witness brought up certain information on the Croatian army and its presence on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1992/1993, the period of the indictment itself. And the Prosecution corroborates this position by saying that it is the Defence who wanted to introduce in this trial a broader contextual approach involving the political, military, and general context. At the beginning, the Prosecution was opposed to this approach, but it was, nevertheless, sanctioned by the Trial Chamber. And now if we approved this broad contextual approach, the Prosecution does not see why Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond they would not be allowed to do so themselves. Now, the second page of the transcript. Can the Defence now present what they have to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence believes that this is not an appropriate way to demonstrate the rights and obligations of the parties to the proceedings as regulated by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. In the indictment, the Prosecution assumed a certain approach on the armed conflict. In the original indictment, this approach was different, and it was modified in the amended indictment. So in it's own case, the Prosecution takes a very narrow approach to events, totally opposed, totally different to the approach of the Defence. Therefore, the questions now being asked by the Prosecution are not linked to their own case and cannot be tied in with Rule 90(H)(ii), because one, count -- cross-examination can rely on examination or, alternatively, it can rely on facts that would be relevant to the party conducting the examination, and neither of these two alternatives applies here, because this questioning does not rely on the arguments presented so far by the Prosecution or the facts brought up in the Prosecution case. Since the Defence has proceeded from the indictment in the context of which the Prosecution says that army forces carried out a frontal attack on Croatian villages, the Defence has exercised its rights from Rule 90(H)(ii) and relied on the events in which these took place. This context follows the theory and the position of the Defence. It is diametrically opposed to the position of the Prosecution. And the Prosecution, by pursuing this line of questioning, is now putting itself in the place of the Defence and we have a total shift in the legal situation here. So this context that has been just brought up by the Prosecution is something that falls in with the theory of the Defence, not of the Prosecution. I believe, therefore, there is no legal basis to pursue this line of questioning. If the witness is asked any more of these questions, it can only serve for the purpose of disqualifying, discrediting the witness. Thank you. I apologise. I believe that this wasn't quite correctly interpreted. I said that if the witness is not telling the truth, then in order to discredit him or to prove the opposite of what he is saying, the Prosecution can possibly show him his written statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the other Defence team like to make any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we don't have any comments to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Prosecution will respond, but I will summarise the debates. We'll be discussing the matter. We will withdraw to discuss the issues raised. I will now provide you with a summary. The Defence has stated that in a certain sense the Prosecution is taking over Defence's arguments with regard to contextual issues. Defence counsel argues that the context is part of their strategy, not part of the Prosecution's strategy. You added that these statements could add to discrediting the within. That's what you said. So, Mr. Mundis, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just three very brief points, if I might. First, we're not relying on Rule 90(H)(ii) in this case. But as we indicated earlier and as Your Honour pointed out in summarising our position. It was the witness himself who first mentioned the term Croatian army, and our view is simply if the witness in responding to a question even during cross-examination brings up an issue we should be permitted to explore that issue, otherwise cross-examination could be meaningless. In the second point, let me just address briefly the issue of strategy, Prosecution strategy or Defence strategy. The Prosecution's strategy, Mr. President, is simply to assist the Trial Chamber in finding out what the truth is. Given the Trial Chamber's previous rulings that it -- that the context is important, we believe it's important for you to have this information as well. And again, the line of questioning I was going to put to the witness would have been over several minutes ago had we been allowed to continue, but it's not a question of strategy here, Mr. President. It's a question of the Chamber has indicated in its previous rulings that context would be important and helpful, and this is simply one more bit of the context that we believe is -- is helpful for the benefit of the Trial Chamber. That's actually it. I'll skip the third point. I don't have much more in terms of cross-examination. We'll hit on this subject and perhaps one or two others, but I should be able to finish relatively quickly with this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you're on your feet, because we want to withdraw. Would you like to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to add something, Mr. President. I think it is important to make further submissions before the Chamber withdraws. With your leave, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. President. The issue we're debating, we can argue about this but that's not the point. The point is that the Trial Chamber rendered a decision with regard to certification, and in this decision the Chamber said that the Trial Chamber cannot declare itself about the nature itself of the conflict, whether it's international or national. The Trial Chamber also adds that if it would be concluded that the conflict was internal, then the question of context would be extremely important for the Defence. Now, Mr. President, the Prosecution has been trying to prove that the conflict was international. My colleague said that in the indictment, in the first indictment, there was the notion of an international armed conflict. This notion was voluntarily withdrawn by the Prosecution. For two years now this idea of an international or internal conflict as a result of an erroneous policy on the part of the Prosecution is making us waste a lot of time. We're now having to deal with a witness who has nothing to do with this, and we're trying to prove that the Croatian army was present there. If the Prosecution wants to change its thesis yet again - and it has done this on numerous occasions in the course of these Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond proceedings - they can do so in the course of the rebuttal phase. When the Defence has finished its case the Prosecution can do this. If they think it's important they can go back to the issue and say we want to prove the existence of international armed conflict. So they can do at that moment. But we shouldn't be drawn into this. We shouldn't be deceived by the Prosecution saying that all we want to do, all the Prosecution wants to do is to help the Chamber determine the truth. We have to respect the rights of the accused. We have to ensure the integrity of the proceedings and of this Tribunal. We mustn't allow the Prosecution to pursue another line of questioning, to move to another subject which will result in the waste of a lot of time and will violate the rights of the accused. Please take into consideration our objection and do not allow this line of questioning. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have lost another ten or 15 minutes now because we've been debating about this since noon. Mr. Bourgon, you raised the issue of the fundamental rights and the necessity of establishing whether it was international or an internal conflict. You said that in the decision rendered the Trial Chamber ruled on certain issues contained in the indictment relating to the nature of this conflict, relating to whether it was international or an internal one. You said the Prosecution would be able to raise this issue after the presentation of the Defence case. Mr. Mundis, as this is a legal issue, which may not be clear to those who are not familiar with it, could you make some comments and then we will withdraw, and we will tell you whether we will allow you to follow this line of questioning. Please respond. This is an important legal issue raised by Mr. Bourgon. Tell us your position and then we will withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As the Trial Chamber is aware this has arisen on several previous occasions primarily in the form of written pleadings. Our position has been clearly articulated that the Office of the Prosecution does not characterise armed conflict. We don't take a position on whether it's an international or internal, non-international armed conflict until the completion of the case, at which point we will then be in a position to argue the law based on the evidence that the Trial Chamber has heard. So our position is that we do not make such characterisations, and our position will remain as it has remained based on the written pleadings that have been filed since this case has begun. So the Prosecution believes that the proper time for making these type of determinations is at the end of the trial based on the evidence that's been heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quarter past twelve. We'll have the break now, and we will resume at about quarter to one, and then we will continue until 2.00. After the break, we'll inform you of our decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber will now render its oral decision with regard to whether the Prosecution will be allowed to follow its line of questioning about the presence of the Croatian army in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Trial Chamber notes that the witness voluntarily, at page 17, line 12, mentioned the presence of the Croatian army. The Chamber, without prejudice to the parties, in relation to the nature of the conflict will allow the Prosecution to put questions concerning the presence of the Croatian army in Bosnia, that is to say in Central Bosnia. The Trial Chamber does not intend to render a non-oral decision stating whether the Prosecution has the right to ask a question that has to do with the nature of the conflict in the course of the Defence's case. The Chamber will not declare its position at this point in time. If the Defence believes that such questions should be excluded in the course of the presentation of its case, Defence counsel may submit a written motion to the Trial Chamber in which -- to which the Prosecution may respond in writing so that a written decision may be rendered. Mr. Mundis, I will now give you the floor, and you may continue, if you so wish, to put questions to the witness we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, before the break I was asking you questions about the HV, that is the Army of the Republic of Croatia. Can you tell us, based on your experience in Central Bosnia in 1992 and 1993, the full extent of HV activity in that region during that time period?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: All I can do is repeat what I have already said. At the beginning, when the presence of the Croatian units were noticed, you could see HV, the sign HV on the vehicles. I also noticed two tanks that were heading in the direction of Jajce. But I can say that the 1st Krajina Battalion that we are discussing, when this battalion arrived in Travnik, Filip Filipovic immediately requested that there be discussions with the -- this command. He wanted it to be said that they'd been sent from Croatia and that they were Croatian soldiers who were being sent to assist the HVO. However, after he said this, this same unit was lined up in the Travnik barracks, and I said that Colonel Filip Filipovic was not right. The role of the HVO there was quite different, and I said that the Territorial Defence wanted to liberate territory that had been occupied by the Serbian and Montenegrin army. They then agreed not to be part of the HVO. They agreed to be part of the Territorial Defence. And this was the case for all 520 men in the battalion. Another example is the HMP units, Croatian Muslim units were sent from Croatia also in the direction of Travnik. This unit was also armed by Croatia. That's where the weapons came from. Of those weapons taken to Travnik, out of those weapons -- we had to distribute them -- we had to distribute half of them to Territorial Defence members and half of them to the Croatian Muslim unit. So this also shows that certain units did come from Croatia, but as far as I am aware, since I spoke to the wife of my brother who died in Ahmici, I also found out in this way that these people weren't local people, they had come from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you aware of any logistical support provided by the Republic of Croatia to these units in Central Bosnia, and if so, can you tell us about that logistical support?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Well, I know for a fact that they received support in arms from Blank page inserted to ensure the pagination between the English and French transcripts correspond Croatia, because if we in the Territorial Defence did not have any weapons because all of the weaponry had been destroyed in Slimena, they got perfectly good infantry weapons, and they got it from Croatia. As for other materiel and equipment, they had no problem in receiving it from Croatia. The equipment didn't have any problem in passing through to them. In other occasions, we could not get equipment because it was seized on the way. Food supplies sometimes couldn't get through. I sent trucks that went to Croatia, to Zagreb, so that they could bring humanitarian supplies to us. I know, on the other hand, for a fact that they were extremely well-armed. Every soldier had state-of-the-art weaponry, the best that was available in those parts at weaponry, the best that was available in those parts at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this state-of-the-art weaponry came from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about any type of support with respect to airlifts or helicopter transport?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Correct. Correct. Such support existed, especially in the area of Vitez, that is, in the area of Mosunj, or as we called it, the Sand Desert. Helicopters landed all the time carrying support, but it's true that in Central Bosnia some helicopters engaged in combat activity. I saw that personally. We received an assignment during the night to train all our weapons to target those helicopters bringing weapons to Central Bosnia, but we were not successful at all. We didn't manage to bring even one of them down. I was personally present when those helicopters landed with logistical support for the HVO, and I can show you exactly the location where it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let me just ask you two follow-up questions. These helicopters, they were from the Croat army or Croat air force?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Croat air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the time period we're talking about is 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Are you also aware, during 1992 and 1993, of the presence of any senior HV commanders?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: In 1992, I had a meeting with General Tole, T-o-l-e. That was his name. And General Praljak as well. I personally met with them at the headquarters in Travnik, at the staff in Travnik, where General Tole had come to convince me and the commander of Novi Travnik, Mr. Lendo, to proceed with some kind of new scheme of defence organisation, the so-called Central Bosnia command. But we rejected it out of hand because we didn't want to join this or that unit. We had our own superior command. Nevertheless, I talked to Mr. Praljak and Mr. Tole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you tell us who Mr. Praljak and Mr. Tole were at that time during 1992?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I don't know which position Tole occupied, but he had the rank of general. He introduced himself as general. He had received an assignment to establish a command for Central Bosnia. I don't know what was his official position. It's not a detail that he shared with us on that occasion. Neither did General Praljak. So I really couldn't tell which positions they occupied.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We absolutely accept the decision you have taken, but we would kindly appreciate it of our colleague, because his questions are wide-ranging and do not really relate to a subject, if he would indicate if these questions relate to our case or he is investigating on an entirely different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the questions have been limited to the period 1992 and 1993, and I believe it's clear to the witness that we're talking about Central Bosnia. I haven't heard the witness indicate that he's confused by any of the questions. It certainly again goes to the very issues we discussed prior to the brief previous recess. I believe the questions that have been asked comply with the oral decision that was just rendered by the Trial Chamber ten or 12 minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you have a lot more questions on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I just have one question remaining pending the answer, of course, of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir -- sir, you told us that you weren't aware of what positions held by General Praljak and General Tole, but again for purposes of clarity, in 1992 when you met with them, in what armed force were they serving?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I couldn't say that either. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just move on to a couple of final questions that I have for you, sir. In the period from June through November of 1992 when you were serving as the commander of the Territorial Defence in Travnik, who was your chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: In that period, my chief of staff was Zijad Cabar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence, in view of the questions asked on the Croatian army, would you like to ask additional questions, because you have well understood that the right to ask them is granted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my learned friend has in his cross-examination referred to a fact that I want to question the witness on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Ribo, tell us, did you at any time earlier give a statement to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I don't know in which case, but I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, concerning the transcript or, rather, for the record I wish to note that the OTP has, during the break, provided the Defence with a copy of this witness's written statement, and having reviewed it, we notice that the OTP had the obligation to disclose this statement to us earlier in keeping with Rule 68. Now, Your Honours, if you would allow me to show the written statement we just received to the witness to verify whether it is indeed the statement that he gave and signed. It is the English version bearing signatures. We also received a partial translation into B/C/S. So I will only show him the statement so that he can identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your signature, Mr. Ribo?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, now in keeping with Rule 89(F), since the witness has identified his signature on the statement that he has given, in the interests of justice and to confirm the credibility of this witness, I would like to tender this statement into evidence. I'm sorry. Before tendering the document, I would like to ask this witness only one more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, when you were giving this statement to the Prosecution, did you speak truthfully as you did today of the events you were familiar with?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now in keeping with Rule 89(F), I would like this document to be tendered as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. On the admission of this document, do you have anything to say on the part of the Prosecution? But I would like to say also that we are now faced with a statement concerning a certain witness. This statement is used by the Prosecution in a certain way during their examination. The Defence tells us we didn't know about this statement. The Prosecution should have disclosed it to us earlier. Now, the fundamental question is to find out whether the Prosecution is duty-bound to disclose all its material once it has the list of witnesses from the moment the Defence has disclosed its list of witnesses, the Prosecution should conduct a search of all its material and disclose everything that pertains to those witnesses. Obviously this is not the way the Prosecution works. Mr. Mundis, could you clarify the situation with this material that appears sporadically, on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence, in their disclosure provisions, do not, in our respectful submission, require us to provide material that our searches come up with with respect to Defence witnesses unless that material, of course, falls within the scope of Rule 68, in which case it should have been turned up by the electronic searches done prior to trial. The Prosecution is, quite frankly, at a loss to understand what in this statement might constitute Rule 68 for purposes of disclosure to the Defence. But leaving that point aside and perhaps my learned colleagues can point me to something that is Rule 68 and which would have fallen within the search terms that we use to electronically search the millions of pages we have our possession to determine what it is Rule 68, perhaps we can do that at a slightly later point, but the fact is, Mr. President, we do our searches, as I've informed the Chamber previously, and those search results quite often come shortly before, perhaps the day before the witness actually testifies. These -- this material quite often is contained in a binder or several binders, simply because we at that point do a search on the names of the witnesses. Due to the fact that we get the Defence witness list shortly before the Defence began its case, it's not possible for us to have these searches done on all the witnesses. We only do them with respect to the witnesses coming for the next week, or we prioritise them in terms of that, which is why it's been a problem as we get relatively late notice as to the witnesses. But there is, pursuant to our reading of the rules and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, no requirement for us to disclose those search results at all to the Defence unless it falls within Rule 68. And as I previously said, I -- looking at this statement now, it's not clear to me that it would -- that it would have been captured by the search terms that we used for purposes of Rule 68. As this Chamber and the Defence are aware, given the fact that we have conducted a number of so-called flip-side cases, Blaskic, Kordic and Cerkez, Furundzija, et cetera, there is a huge, huge amount of material concerning the conflict in Central Bosnia, and for us to disclose that in its totality to the Defence would mean this trial would have to grind to a stop so that they could review all of that material. Our obligations are limited by Rule 68; we believe we have complied with that. Now, if the Defence can point us to something in here that should have fallen within the parameters of our Rule 68 obligations then we can address that problem and perhaps take whatever steps need to be taken, but the point of the matter or the fact of the matter is I generally get these search results shortly before the witness comes. We don't believe we are entitled or required to provide that to the Defence. If the Chamber, however, rules otherwise, we will take whatever steps are necessary, but that could result in a huge amount of information being disclosed to the Defence shortly before, the day before, or perhaps even the day the witness testifies. I can't predict when we actually get this search material into my own hands, let alone be in a position to disclose it to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to give you the floor, but there -- is there an objection to the admission of this document into evidence? The Defence has asked for this document to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. No, there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A few seconds if you want to say something.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just before I do, can I ask this witness one question, and then I will respond to my learned friend?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ribo, regarding what you said before this Trial Chamber and what you stated in the written statement, could you tell us, did HVO, in 1992 and 1993, dispose of forces that far outnumbered and out-powered the forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: In view of their level of equipment and their materiel and supplies, it is certainly the case that they were much better equipped technically, and they were far superior to the army whose equipment, especially weaponry, were extremely scarce.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the statement that we have tendered confirms precisely what the witness just said. The Defence has from the outset pointed out the balance of power in the context of the conflict in Bosnia, and the Prosecution has, therefore, known that it had in its possession statements of officers of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which support this theory of the Defence. Therefore, Rule 68 does not relate only to the appearance of Defence evidence. It obliges the Prosecution to disclose before the trial such statements of officers of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina so that -- so as to enable the Defence to investigate, to locate, and identify those officers. Fortunately, we located this witness through our own efforts and brought him to this courtroom. It is, therefore, our opinion that Rule 68 can by no means be linked to the lists of witnesses we supply to the Prosecution. It is connected with the facts that impose certain obligations on the OTP from the moment of issue of the indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have now entered a discussion on Article 68. Mr. Mundis, I can give you a few more seconds to reply if you wish. However, I'm looking at the clock, and I am aware of the fact that we have another witness waiting. Mr. Mundis, I'm not going to deprive you of the time if you wish to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm also aware of the time and I'm trying to do the best I can. Let me just say one thing, though, with respect to what my learned colleague has just said about the Defence position and the applicability of Rule 68 to that position. With all due respect, Mr. President, virtually, if not every, member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina will say exactly what this witness just said with respect to the HVO having superior weaponry and logistical support. The phrase that she just put to the -- or the question she put to the witness and the underlying information that's contained in this witness statement is by no means unique to this witness. You could find any, any soldier who served in the ABiH in Central Bosnia and every single one of them will tell you the same thing, that the HVO had far more resources in terms of weaponry and equipment. There is nothing in this statement that particularly is Rule 68 with respect to this case. And second of all, as the Defence knows we conduct our Rule 68 searches electronically, and the concept, the notion she just put to the witness is not something that can be easily searched electronically in terms of the concept of who was superior to whom. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence counsel, do you have any questions to put which would arise from the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. We do not have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges are going to ask you a few questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to put you one or two very simple questions on a document in relation to what you said this morning about the Muslim forces in Travnik. You told us that the Muslim forces were founded in August 1992, that you were surprised to hear that, and that you were also angry to -- of that fact, because that did not apparently make your duties easier. I have a document relating to the establishment of these forces in August in Travnik, 1992, and I would like to put you some questions about it, and I would like to ask the registrar to give you the original text. It's a Prosecution document, P695. Would you please have a look at it. You may note that on the first page in the original document, and there is a date, 15th of September of 1992, and at the end of the document there is a signature of Emir Redzic, whose name you mentioned this morning. And the document is about a list of soldiers of the Travnik Muslim forces. Please look at the document before I put you a few detailed -- questions of detail on it. Have you been able to look at it?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Is this the same Emir Redzic you spoke about earlier this morning?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: He is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: If I look at the first page, I have a little bit uncertitude about who is sending what to whom. I suppose that Mr. Redzic is sending a list of names of soldiers of the Travnik Muslim forces to the Travnik armed forces staff, but since I do not know your language, I would like to verify that. Is that the purpose of the letter, to send something to the Travnik armed forces staff?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And my next question would be: The Travnik armed forces staff, is this something different from the territorial municipal organisations you spoke about this morning or is it the same body or -- please explain to me whether there is a difference or whether this is in fact the organisation you were the head of in 1992.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: It's the same body that I headed once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Did you ever receive the document?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I may have. I'm not sure. There are many bodies within my command. It could have been sent to one of those bodies. These bodies were independent. Logistics people could write certain instructions, orders, et cetera. Even the chief of security could do that, especially the officer in charge of personnel could draft such documents, affix stamps, request certain data. So this list didn't necessarily pass through my hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you look again at the first page of the original document, it's something that surprises me given the comments you have made this morning on the establishment of this unit. If I'm not mistaken, but please correct me if I'm mistaken, the person who sends this letter or this list to the Travnik armed forces staff, Mr. Redzic, is making use of the name of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that right, or do I interpret the text in an incorrect way?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: Let me tell you, there were no rules about the cover letters, and there were no rules concerning the drafting of these letters. The heading is the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I don't know whether this was already legalised. We still had Territorial Defence. I don't know whether the army existed at the time or not. However, I can only tell you that we did not have any rules as to how to word the -- the covers, and every unit had its own rules. Letterheads were not uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: But it gives the impression by using the name of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the left top side, followed by Travnik Muslim forces and then a date, he gives the impression to the reader of this letter that he belongs to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: They didn't belong to me. I did not make a decision to send the formation. My superior command did not make a decision to establish it, so they could have put anything they wanted. The stamp that you see here was the same thing that was on uniforms. They could have put whatever they wanted to. However, there was no single enactment directed either by myself or my superior command that would say that they would have been established by the territorial staff or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Proper way of sending a letter. He had no right to refer to himself as part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's your answer. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: That's correct. Precisely that. I can confirm what you have just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question to put to you. This morning you spoke about the first conflict that started in Turbe, and you said that there were some troops on the ground, and I quote you, you said that you saw the MUP, the Green Berets, the Patriotic League, and volunteers from the village. What are you tell us about the Green Berets? Who are they?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: In -- let me -- let me put it simply. I don't know who they were. They just wore green hats. They were volunteers, to my mind, and I don't know anything else about them, to be honest. This Defence line was attacked by the Serbians and Montenegrins, and it was defended by the Croatian people together with these other people. So I really don't know. I wouldn't be able to tell you. I wasn't in Bosnia at the moment when the Patriotic League forces were formed and when Green Berets were established. There was always a gap between us, between us in the staff and the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. They claim that they are the ones that organised the resistance, but I wouldn't be able to tell you anything else about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. After the two questions put to the witness by the Judges, do you have any questions to clarify any matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ribo, Judge Swart has shown you this document and you said that the signatory is Emir Redzic, for whom you've heard that he was their commander. Do you know who the people in the letter are, and did the Municipal Staff ever issue orders to them?

utterances.speaker: HASO RIBO
utterances.text: I don't know who these people are. I don't know who the people on the list are. I never issued any orders of any sort to these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ribo, your testimony hereby finishes. We would like to thank you for having come to testify, for having answered the questions put to you by the Defence, by the Prosecution, and the Judges. We wish you a happy journey back home, and we wish you luck in your present profession. I'm going to ask the usher to accompany you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And while the usher is accompanying the witness out of the courtroom, I'm going to give the floor to the Defence and ask them to tender the eight documents that they have presented today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we would like to tender the following documents as Defence exhibits: 0410, 0440, 0446, 0457, 0486, 0487, 0489, and 0490. I would like to point out that document number 0440 can be found within the Prosecutor's exhibit P120. This exhibit is the entire of the Official Gazette. However, this document has not been translated and has not been marked for identification. That's why the Defence believes that this document should be also admitted as a Defence exhibit under number 0440.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Mr. Registrar, can you please give me eight numbers for these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The first document is going to be DH410, and the English version will be DH410/E; The second -- the second document will be DH413; the third document will be 446, and the English translation will be 446/E; the fourth document is DH457, and the English translation 457/E; the next one DH486, English translation DH486/E; the next one DH487, and the English translation DH487/E; the next document is DH489, and the English translation 489/E; and the last document, DH490, and the English translation 490/E. And finally, the witness's statement is admitted as DH343.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I don't know the witness was going to come in so quickly. But we were going to ask as the Defence, I know time is pressing but if we might have simply a five-minute break before this witness starts, there's one matter we need to address with the Defence and also with my learned friend from the Prosecution. I think it'll help the testimony thereafter. I'm sorry to interrupt but I would be grateful for five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want a five-minute break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's our request before the witness commences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness may be seated. We will just leave the courtroom for five minutes and then we will continue. Is that what you desire, Mr. Dixon?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you may be seated we are coming back in a few minutes. --- Short break taken at 1.41 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you please hear me? If yes, can you say so? Can you say, I understand, I hear you and I understand you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can hear you and I can understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called as a Defence witness. Before you take the solemn declaration, I need to find out your name. Can you please give us your name, your family name, and can you tell us where and when you were born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Halim Husic. I was born on 25 September, 1958, in Dub near Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession? What do you currently do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently I am a history teacher in the religious school in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, what is your profession? If you were a military, can you please tell us what unit you belonged to and what rank did you have at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, I joined the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a foot soldier. Then I was appointed assistant commander for moral guidance, information, propaganda, and religious matter in the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before an International Tribunal or before a national court on the events that took place in 1992 and 1993 in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have never testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a new question that I ask the witnesses from now on: Have you ever given a statement to the Prosecution of this Tribunal? Have you ever signed a written statement for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have not given a written statement. However, a year ago - I can't remember the exact date - a gentleman whose name I cannot remember asked to talk to me. We had an interview in Sarajevo, and this is all that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this gentleman belonged to the Prosecutor's office? He was one of their investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His name was Michael Koehler. I believe so, but I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I'm now going to ask you to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still have ten minutes before the break that we have to make for technical reasons. We have been sitting since 9.00, and after the break we will resume at 3.00. I would like to make the most of these ten minutes to give you some information about how your testimony is going to take place. You're going to answer the questions put by the Defence counsel, who are on your left. After that, you're going to be questioned by the Prosecution seated on your right. Once the Prosecution is finished with their cross-examination, the Defence will be given the floor for re-examination. The Prosecutor may reply and put some additional questions to you after that. The three Judges who are seated before you can ask you questions at any moment. As a rule, they prefer to wait until the end, after all the questions have been put by both sides for them to ask questions. However, if they need clarification immediately, if they need to fill a gap, the Judges may ask you questions at any point in time. The questions may be complicated. The questions may rely on your memory of the events that took place over ten years ago. If you do not understand a question or if you do not remember, can you please indicate that? Can you ask the person who put the question to rephrase it? If there are any other difficulties, do not hesitate to ask for our assistance and we'll try to deal with the issue. I would like to inform you of two other elements that are very important and that may have an impact on your testimony. You have declared that you will tell the truth and nothing but the truth, which means that you are not allowed to give a false testimony. If it appears that you have not told us the truth, you may be liable for false -- for punishment for false testimony, and the punishment for that may be up to seven years in prison. The other element that is important and that may have a bearing on a member of the military in 1992 or 1993 is as follows: It may happen that while replying to a question, you may feel like you might incriminate yourself. At this moment, I would like to tell you that your words used here today ask not be used against you, because you will be given a sort of immunity by this Tribunal. I'm telling you this just to encourage you to tell us the whole truth. And this is in very general terms how the testimony is going to develop. But since we are coming to the break, I would like to ask you to come back after the break. We don't want to break the rhythm of your testimony. We are going to make a break of one hour for technical reasons and to give the opportunity to everybody in the courtroom to have a little rest and recharge their batteries for the afternoon session. So we will now break and resume at 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.55 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence, I would like to say to the parties that the interpreters have let me know that they cannot stay longer than 5.00. Theoretically, we have -- so that the interpreters can stay no longer than 6.00. We have three hours. We're going to have a 20-minute break, but I would like to ask both parties to be very economical with the time, because we don't want the witness to stay over the weekend. So I want both parties to understand that we want to be economical with the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence will try and respect that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Husic, good afternoon?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to try and answer my questions as precisely as possible, and if there is anything you don't understand, can you please ask me to rephrase my question. Tell me, please, you've already told us where and when you were born. Can you now tell us, please, what schools you finished and what you did before the war.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: After the primary school in Dub, I went to Gazi Husrev Beg's medresa in Sarajevo. That is a secondary school. And then I went on to study at the religious university in Sarajevo. And then I started working at the same address where I graduated from. I started teaching history, and this is where I was until the moment the aggression was launched against Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So I would say that you are a teacher of theology, is that correct, of religious education?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where were you at the beginning of April 1992? Where did you reside before the war and where were you at the moment when the war started at the beginning of April 1992?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Before the war I resided in Sarajevo, where I worked. And when the aggression was launched against Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was away on business in Umag, a little town in Croatia not far from Trieste. I stayed there for 40 days and this is when the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started, and that is why I was prevented from returning. It took me over a month to go back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, after the 40 days that you spent there, did you return to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I couldn't go back to Sarajevo because Sarajevo was completely blocked. I got as far as Kiseljak near Sarajevo. I spent some ten days there because it was not possible to -- for me to go either to Travnik or to Sarajevo from there. After those ten days or so, I used some channels. I was helped with -- by some people. One of them was a Croat, and they helped me to get to my parents' house, which was in Han Bila, a place near Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, at any point in time did you become a member of the armed forces, and that is the case, what armed forces were those and when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: On the 16th of May, the same day when I returned, I became a member of the armed forces. That was in 1992. When I arrived in my parents' house where my brothers also lived, and I hadn't seen them in months before that, my brother was at school in Han Bila. He was at that moment lined up, and he was supposed to go to the lines on Mount Vlasic, on the lines facing Serbians and Montenegrins. I made the most of that moment to say hello to him before he left. I met with some of my friends there, and I stayed with them. We talked about the situation in Bila. I volunteered, and five days later, I was on the front line as a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, what arms did you have, and what about the other members of the Territorial Defence, and where did you get the weapons from?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: At the beginning there was very few weapons. Some of those weapons were obtained and purchased through -- through smugglers, channels. This came from the Serbian population that had been armed by the JNA. The rest of the weapons in our area was taken from the JNA depot that had been burnt down by the JNA as they were leaving. While the depot was still burning, people went there. Some people even lost their feet and hands. They went there to collect weapons. Some of the weapons were reclaimed from the burnt depot, so some of the machine-guns exploded in our faces because they had been heavily burned. And there was also some handmade weapons. For example hand grenades were made of cans that were used for Coca-Cola and beer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, at any point in time from Han Bila or from the defence positions that you were sent to, did you go to Travnik, and did you get acquainted with the initiative on the establishment of other forces which were not Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: After my return to the area where I was born, after having spent a lot of time on Vlasic, when I returned home, I wanted to obtain a uniform because my clothes were not suitable. At that time, there was very little by way of uniforms. I went there to purchase a uniform. I met a lot of friends of mine and my acquaintances that I knew from before, and we were talking about the establishment of some other forces because -- there was a lot of talk about the establishment of some groups that called themselves the MOS, the Muslim Liberation Forces. However, when I saw that these groups were made up of very young people, people who very often or at least some of them were my former students, some of them had graduated only that year, which means that they had not been trained as soldiers. When I spoke to my friends and my acquaintances, I would tell them that this was not a good situation, that I am not very sure, but their -- that their willingness to fight should be put to a bad use and that whatever we wanted to do we should do within the scope of the organisation that already existed in Travnik municipality, and that these young boys should take part in the fighting by joining those units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, what did your acquaintances and friends mention as their reasons for which they wanted to establish those so-called Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Before that, in their -- in that area there were units that were called HOS. Because of the fact that in Bosnia everything functions proportionally, the Croatian forces initiated the establishment of the Muslim forces. And similar things happened with other things like insignia, the hanging flags on buildings, certain emblems and symbols that were worn on uniforms. This was all based on the so-called principle of proportionality, and a lot of units were formed in that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you offered at that time to join the initiators of this, and what was your training?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Some of these people invited me to join them, and that's why they mentioned the initiative in the first place. However, we disagreed on the basic concept, because my view was that these young people isolated into separate units would probably be killed very quickly. And some of them, as I said, were my students. And as their former teacher, I could not agree to such an offer, and that's why I returned to the Territorial Defence. This decision of mine bothered my parents, for example, because the experiences in Central Bosnia with -- with the Second World War and the participation of Muslim population in the Second World War were not positive, and it was expected, yet once again, that the Territorial Defence, which would later on become the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, would become something that Partisans were in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your very extensive answer. Mr. Husic, can you now please tell us did you at any point in time in 1992 met or see -- meet or see some foreigners that had arrived in Travnik? If that is the case, can you tell us what foreigners were those, and especially can you tell us whether you had some encounters with foreigners from Arabic or northern African states?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: At that time, Travnik was swamped with foreigners for a simple reason: A lot of refugees came to Travnik from all other the place, so among those foreigners there were members of the UNPROFOR, European Monitors, journalists of all nationalities. But I spent a lot of time on Mount Vlasic. However, there was a small group of people of Arabic origin, and you could actually tell who they were by the clothes they wore. They were later on located in at a place called Mehuric. We use to call and refer to them as Arabs, and later on they would become known as the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, you have just told us that all that time you were on the defence lines on Mount Vlasic. When and where was it that you first saw such individuals, the individuals that you referred to as Arabs? Did you and where did you see these persons?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The first time I saw them was in Mehurici where the principal of the primary school was a cousin of mine, Muradif Husic. When he was given the task to accommodate Arabs, and there was also the command of the detachment there, he called me, hoping that I would help him interpret into -- into the Arabic, and he wanted my help. However, when I arrived, I couldn't communicate with these people. A dozen of them were then accommodated in the school in Mehurici, and from then onwards when I occasionally arrived in Mehurici where I had to go quite often, I could see that a number of them still worked and lived in that place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, can you please tell the Honourable Chamber what these people looked like? How did they differ from other foreigners who arrived in your area? And also, you as an imam, as a theologist, as a religious official, what did you in 1992 know about these so-called Arabs or Mujahedins?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: My education took me to the Arabic world on several occasions, and I was well acquainted with the Arabic people, the way they were dressed and they spoke, and they looked like. I knew much more than the villagers of Mehurici or any other locals. As far as their arrival and accommodation in Mehurici is concerned and which was very certain is that they delivered a lot of aid, particularly food, because already at that time a lot of people were on the verge of starvation because of the lack of food. The second part or other Arabs were engaged in education, and in almost all the villages around Mehurici they opened schools. I was also offered to work in one of those schools together with my wife who had been trained in the same way as myself. However, our condition was that this education should use Bosnian textbooks. They didn't accept this, so we refused to be engaged. The third segment of that group was engaged in the organisation and -- of the delivery of weapons and military uniforms. And later on they started training other people, because the population of that area, because of the assistance that had been extended to them and the trust that they gained in these people, started sending their children to those schools and later on for training that was occasionally organised. It was military training.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, you have just told us that they offered you to join them. What did they offer you in more specific terms?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: They asked both my wife and myself to work in their schools that they opened. We refused to do that. Later on as a member of the 306th Mountain Brigade, in a conversation with them, I was again offered, although our salary in the Bosnian army was 4 convertible marks a month, I was offered 2.000 German marks to join them, to join their ranks. Again I turned the offer down. And this was one of my last conversations with them, because again I was not very happy with their behaviour, and I did not agree with the way they acted in the Bila valley. I told them that. And because of that, our contacts became few and far between.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just go back to one part of the answer that you have just given us. You told us that they provided assistance and later on that they even distributed weapons. Who did they provide assistance to? Who did they give money to? Who was it that they invited for these training exercises in their camp?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Like any other humanitarian organisations, Arabic organisations also delivered assistance to people personally. They didn't go through the official channels. To a large extent, they were engaged on the delivery of food to the entire population of the area, especially to those who were in very dire straits. As far as the military equipment and weapons are concerned, since the military equipment and weapons were smuggled all over the place, you could obtain weapons everywhere at very high prices. They used some people as mediators to obtain weapons, and the training that they organised involved volunteers who volunteered to stay with them and undergo such training.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, did you at any point in time take over a certain duty or position in any of the units of the BiH army? If that is the case, can you please tell us what position it was and when you took it?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Having spent some time in Ljuta Bila, when the 306th Mountain Brigade was established I became assistant commander for moral guidance and religious affairs in the 306th Mountain Brigade. From then on, from the month of November 1992 up to November 1993, I performed those duties and tasks. Up to the end of November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Husic, what was the area from which the troops were recruited into the units of the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: People for the 306th Brigade were recruited from the area of the Bila valley. This is what we called this part of the Travnik municipality. That was the order at the beginning, which came from the 3rd Corps. We were ordered to establish the 306th mountain brigade from the forces that had already existed in the Bila valley. Those were the 1st Detachment, which was deployed in the Mehurici school, the so-called Siprage Detachment;then the Ljuta Greda Detachment and the Han Bila Detachment and a detachment which later on became the 2nd Battalion in the area of Krpeljic. Its name was the LG Detachment. However, at the time when this order was supposed to be executed, some problems arose. Certain individuals, for personal or some other reasons, did not want to be recruited in that way. They did not want to -- the brigade to be established in that way. Some other individuals who also were active in the valley managed to have some of the population which was from Gluha Bukovica, Zagrdje, and Skomorje, joined the 314th Brigade that was headquartered in Zenica. The departure of some of the population that should have been recruited for the 306th Mountain Brigade caused a certain reaction against other units. So despite the order and the deadline for establishment of the 306th brigade, we had this brigade on paper only for months, and it was very difficult to establish it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can I please show the witness a binder of documents that I will be using in the rest of my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, can you please look at this document under number 1 in the first part of this binder. Mr. Husic, in December 1992, did you know about this request? Were you aware of it? Does it reflect the things that you have just testified about?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I was aware of this request. Because of the problems that I've mentioned, I visited every village. I talked to the members of these detachments and the request forwarded by the Mehurici squadron to the corps was their reaction in disagreement to the things that were being done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. A little while ago, you told us that that the 306th Brigade should have been replenished from the Bila valley but some of the population joined the 314th Brigade and other brigades. Tell me, please, this fact that more than one brigades were replenished from one area and their commands were not in the area but in some other areas, did this fact cause certain problems for the 306th Brigade? Did this cause some confusion, impossibility to identify people, and similar things?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. The fact that some of the population that resided and/or 12 originated from the Bila valley joint other units, particularly units whose commands were not in the vicinity, were not within an easy reach, enabled a number of prospective conscripts to evade military service. Their excuse would be that they belonged to another unit, and that's how for months they managed to avoid any engagement. All that time, they behaved in a way which the rest of the population found revolting. In addition to that, the movement of these groups in the -- in the area where we resided caused problems among the Muslim population. But also when the checkpoints were put up by the HVO every time that they moved to and from the Bila valley there were incidents. On the other hand, in our area there were a lot of refugees, some of whom --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, can you please slow down so that the interpreters could follow you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
