utterances.text: Some of the combatants who had previously been in the units where they lived after they had been expelled arrived together with their families in the Bila river valley, and that is how a large number of armed population who moved around this entire area was outside of any control, in particular, at the time when HVO would mount a blockade, because all three potential exits from the valley, from as early as New Year's, I'm referring to New Year's 1993, HVO held under their control all of these access routes, and every passage had to be announced in advance with all the details in terms of number of armed individuals and so on and so forth. We, who held the line against Serbs and Montenegrins, we knew about their cooperation, and the fact that our men would be in advance counted together with the weapons was a significant problem for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to the problem concerning the individuals who appeared from time to time in your area but were not members of your brigade. The 306th Brigade and its organs, could it establish with any amount of certainty who these individuals who were moving around the area were, and did you encounter identification and investigation related problems, and were there also cases of false identification?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Those were very common problems for the 306th. Very often, we would wrongly establish the identity of certain individuals. We would inform the command of the corps thereon, and after the investigation, we would learn, for instance, that the members whom we had considered to be members of the 7th Muslim Brigade were not members of that brigade, as was the case with many other individuals because of the fact that the 7th Muslim Brigade had been replenished from a very wide area and their headquarters were not in our vicinity, so we were not able to check. Those individuals would introduce themselves of that unit where in actual point of fact they were members of some other units, and many of them were not members of any unit at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In light of that very difficult problem, were any measures taken at any point in time in 1993 in order to carry out adequate identification of combatants and establish whether they were actually members of armija?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Since the negotiations with the HVO took place, we tried to convince them that with the help of the corps, we were able to establish control over the movements of our members but also the movement of any other armed individuals. Very often, long-barrelled weapons, we insisted that they be on the line, on the front line, which was rarely -- which sometimes was not accepted. We also had the problem with identification of uniforms and the insignia. The insignia were simply not enough for the purposes of identification. So it was on the basis of both weapons and insignia that we did this work. But this was all manipulated, because the uniform was worn by a number of civilians as well who were not members of any other unit. And we also had a large number of combatants who did not have uniform, and that is how it was not -- and that is why it was not possible for us to conduct identification. We insisted on this further, and we wanted to have adequate military cards to be created. But because of the problems with communication, we were very limited, and this all took very, very long.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In order not to discuss other problems that the brigade was facing at the time, tell me simply what was the communication of your brigade with subordinate and superior commands?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, due to the configuration of the terrain of Central Bosnia, the altitude of Vlasic is over 1.900 metres, our defence line on the mount Vlasic were located at the average altitude of 1.500 metres, and Vlasic is infamous for its climate. Bad weather is often the problem, even in the summer, let alone in the winter. Our units were replenished from about 30 inhabited places, and the communication was intersected by HVO units who were able to control the system of communication and the movement at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 94, line 10. The witness indicated that the problem with the identification also was taking photographs and not communication. So I would like to -- this to be corrected, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you have answered also this part of the question. You -- in terms of communication, it was the configuration of the terrain that made the communication difficult.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The communication lines were often severed, but what is from a military point of view a particular problem is the fact that our communication lines were completely covered at all times. It was possible to listen to our communication for them at all times, and we knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber is aware of the fact that Sarajevo was encircled, that it was under siege. And in light of what you have said so far, I should like to know whether you had any direct communication with the staff of the Supreme Command or the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Of course not. Very often we didn't have any communication at all with Travnik and Zenica let alone with Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us please go back to the issue of foreigners whom you encountered in 1992 in the school that you mentioned. Tell us, please, as a member of the command of the 306th, do you know where these foreigners are now? Are you aware of their current whereabouts, and can you tell us whether they are creating problems for your brigade?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I'm not. I don't understand your question. Are you referring to the present time or --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm referring to 1993 because you said in 1992 your cousin called you and it was at that time that they went to the upper floor on that school. After the brigade was established, did you know where those foreigners were, the Mujahedin or the Arabs, whatever you call them. And did their presence create problems for your brigade?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I was confused with the word "now." So after the 306th Brigade was established, one of their battalions, the 1st Battalion, was billeted in the elementary school in Mehurici. They were very arrogant. Their behaviour was arrogant. Those were young men who had been expelled from their villages. They didn't know what the situation was with their families. They had seen terrible things happen to their families. There were still large quantities of alcohol going around in the area. They created problems very often, and that's why these Arabs moved out of the school and took up quarters in abandoned houses in the village of Poljanice in the immediate vicinity of Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You testified a moment ago that they approached the local population in various ways and gained their favour. Tell us, please, is there anything that you would like to add and that you consider to be important, to have been important for you as a member of the command, in connection with the fact that these individuals had certain influence and exerted certain influence on the local population in the area where your brigade was located?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The situation in Bosnia at that time was very difficult. The population was on the brink, and any form of aid or assistance was more than welcome. People waited for a very long time for the international community to recognise what the real situation in Bosnia was and to put a stop to a situation which was amounting to a genocide. When this did not happen, the attitude towards those who provided this type of assistance was getting more positive. And that is how the population became attached to these people. After all, these people were bringing food to the area. They were educating their children in cooperation with our people. So there was this link with the local population which for us as members of the brigade who were not able to provide any help not only to the civilian population but also to the members of the 306th, this brought us in a very difficult situation, and that is why we had all these problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Their way of life, their religious education, and the fact that they were actually taking your youth who were supposed to join the Territorial Defence, was that something that led to conflicts amongst the population, amongst the local residents themselves?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: As far as the strength of the 306th Brigade is concerned, we had a lot of problems. And even if we would have had three times as many people, it would have been difficult to accomplish all the tasks. Part of the population because of the age groups, because of the age of the people who were members of the 306th, made it very difficult for them to withstand the situation, and that's why it was difficult for us to replenish all these units, and this is why we experienced these problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have heard the request of our interpreters, so I kindly ask you to speak slowly, please. Witness, you are an imam, a theologist. Tell us, please, as far as the religious community is concerned, the religious community of the area, were there any problems because of the way the religion was practised, the problems which also affected your brigade?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Islam has been present in Bosnia from the 15th century. The way of practice, the Bosnian way, was something our population has been used to for very long. So certain novelties which were being introduced by these foreigners created a lot of confusion and a lot of problems. And then the official organs of the Islamic Community often reacted because this conduct was disturbing, was a disruption in a long-established way of practising religion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Husic. I believe I have finished this. Were there any other military formations deployed in the area? So will you please first tell me, were there any such formations there, and if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to enumerate all the formations who were there or who were in contact with our area. Ever from the beginning of the armed resistance in the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the units that were created, most of them were just self-armed units from the local area. They had various names, and they would later on constitute the basis from which the staff of the Territorial Defence would later on replenish and establish units which were then officially formed by the relevant authorities. Moreover, the individuals who had been previously engaged in weapons smuggling and were now smuggling food and obviously had money would, from time to time, obtain weapons, equip certain groups, and thus create units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, we discussed this, I think, a moment ago. I would like to know now whether there were any other organised military forces in the area, and I think I can ask directly.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: In addition to the HOS, from the New Year's of 1993 in all of the areas inhabited by the Croat population and acting pursuant to an order issued at the time, home guard units, HVO home guard village units were being established. In April they all joined one single brigade. The Frankopan HVO Brigade whose seat was in Guca Gora. And that is how the Bila river valley actually consisted of two HVO brigades. One part was under the Zenica HVO Brigade, and the other part under the Frankopan HVO Brigade which was headquartered in Guca Gora, which further complicated the situation that I talked about a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, tell us, please, how and in what way it was possible to get out of the Bila river valley, and did a problem arise at one point in time, a problem concerning the communication of people, of population and the military with other parts of the state.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The Bila river valley is a dead-end street in Bosnia, in Central Bosnia. The three roads leading to Travnik and Zenica from the Bila river valley, from January 1993, were continuously under blockade and under the control of the HVO. In some situations, it was possible to pass through with prior notice and authorisation. However, these passages often involved humiliation, harassment and mistreatment, and that is why people hesitated to go through. There were even cases of women giving birth at those passages because they wouldn't be allowed passage. As for the military, every passage had to be announced in advance with detailed description of manpower, equipment, weapons, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this set of documents, I would like you to have a look at document number 6 and also document number 7 from this first batch. And in the second part, you have references at the end, at the bottom, documents 1, 2, and 3 from the second -- from the second batch. And I will have some questions in relation to that. Document number 6 is Defence number 1010, number 7 is Defence document 1043.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have found all these documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's have a look at the document of the 14th of May. It's a document emanating from the 3rd Corps, and it talks about an event which concerns the command of the 306th. Are you familiar with this event?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was one of the captives here, one of the members of the command who were taken prisoner on this occasion. I think I indicated a moment ago that in addition to regular checkpoints and the complete blockade of the Bila river valley, there were also unofficial irregular checkpoints, because armed groups entered the area we moved around, laid ambushes, and engaged in mistreatment, plunder, and various forms of harassment not only against soldiers but against civilians as well. This document concerns the incident where a large number of people from the command of 306th Brigade were taken prisoner. They were ambushed, taken prisoner on a road that we were mistreated. Our van and our lorry were requisitioned. They also took everything, all the equipment that was of any value that we had. Although we didn't have any uniforms, they even took civilian clothes from some of us. So -- and the event took place only one kilometre and a half from the house where I -- where I live and where my family, my children, and my parents lived at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, would you please have a look at document number 7. Tell us, please, if you can skip -- skim through this document, whether you witnessed the events described in this document. Did you know in 1993 that these events had taken place in the way described here?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: This is a report of the 306th Mountain Brigade on the events that had taken place in our area of responsibility. You have a list of events that I am -- that I've been talking about here. From New Year's 1993, not a day passed without an incident. The situation got exacerbated from the 10th of April. The 10th of April is the day of NDH, the Independent State of Croatia. And from there, from that date, until the final showdown between the HVO and the BH army, as I said, not a single day passed without an incident, without a wounded person or without a fatality.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think the document speaks enough for itself, and I can only thank you that you can confirm that you can bear witness to the events that took place. Now I have to apologise but the Trial Chamber appealed to us to use the time as efficiently as possible, so I have to ask you to move to the exhibits in the second part, Exhibits number 1, 2, and 3. Tell us, please, do you recognise these documents as well? They're actually three documents. Do you recognise the events described in these documents as the events that took place in 1993 and the events that you were aware of in 1993? This is the document -- the documents listed after the title "Exhibit."

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. These documents refer to regrouping of forces, and the document under number 3 talks about the same event in connection with this command, and we have a list of items that were requisitions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Husic, I would like to discuss the events which took place in late May, early June. Tell us, in connection to that, where you were on the 1st of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The events which took place between the 1st and the 8th cannot be separated in that way, because intensive fighting had been going on for some time. However, on the 1st of June, after the negotiations in Guca Gora had fallen through, the conflict intensified, and part of the command of the 306th, the commander, assistant commander for moral guidance, assistant commander for finance, who were later joined by the chief of staff who had been brought from Travnik by UNPROFOR, we found ourselves in a complete blockade and cut off from the rest of the world in the village of Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Which part of Guca Gora?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The village of Krpeljici. We were there in a house conducting negotiations, but the actual blockade was in the village of Krpeljici near Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who was with you in Krpeljici who from the command?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sipic, the commander, Mr. Siljak, chief of staff, assistant for financial affairs, Mr. Mujo Husanovic and myself. The seat of the 2nd Battalion was also located in this village, and therefore the commander of the 2nd Battalion was also present when the area was blocked, as was the case with a dozen other villages in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first news that reached you on the events taking place in your area?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Since some of the villages had been under a blockade for over a month, Radojcici, Ricice, Velika Bukovica, when this new wave of violence occurred, all ten villages at this part of the Bila river valley where Bosnian and Croat population was mixed were encircled and blocked, and it was impossible for these villages to have any form of communication, and the blockade in some of the villages such as Radojcici, Ricice and Bukovica had been going on for over a month. It was not possible to do any form of agricultural work. It was not possible for the population to leave their houses. The movement was not possible. And for the past ten days, some of the villages were also being shelled. And the intensity of the conflict was increasing by the day, and Krpeljici also came under heavy shelling from the area --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the name of the area.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Shelled from rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive news at any point in time about the attacks of the HVO? In which area, and with what consequences?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The blockade of the part of the command in Krpeljici meant the beginning of a new wave of very violent fighting, which included, apart from shelling and sniping, machine-gun fire which was opened on all of these villages, including Krpeljici where we were. However, the most intensive fighting took place in the village of Velika Bukovica where the local population who were defending themselves against ten times stronger HVO forces, there was a large number of fatalities and casualties, and the population kept asking us, the command, for help. It was not possible to provide them with any assistance. They were running out of ammunition, and their fate was uncertain. As for Ricice, their population fled towards Han Bila. Request for help with an emphasis on food and not ammunition came from the village of Radojcici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, what is your personal knowledge of what was happening on the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of June, at one moment the whole Bila valley, one can say, was aflame. The shooting that one could hear from all other the place and from time to time became more intense. And on that particular day, it was very intense. We didn't know what was going on. And like on the previous days, we cried for help. We sent requests for help to the 3rd Corps, but we did not receive any reply. And as a matter of fact, the only thing we could do was to instruct every village to defend themselves with what little strength they have. After that, we received information that our forces, which we kept in reserve because of the intense cooperation between the Serbians and Montenegrins and the HVO which started at that day, around that time, warned us that an attack could come from Mount Vlasic which we could not be able to repel or sustain, because we did not have ammunition. As a result of that, these forces which from the area of Mehurici via Konska [phoen], which is in the direction of Mount Vlasic, started moving and linked up with the 2nd Battalion, and that meant that Velika Bukovica, that the blockade was lifted from Velika Bukovica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, where were you, on which combat axis? Actually, did you join the combat activities? Did you engage in combat, and what axis did you move on in the next following days?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: These forces that I have just mentioned, they linked up with the 2nd Battalion from Krpeljici, and after that happened, in front of us was Guca Gora from which there was an intense fire being opened on Krpeljici and other places. This was the seat of the Frankopan Brigade. The shelling lasted four days before that. So our next target was Guca Gora. However, it turned out that the population had fled Guca Gora during the previous night so our forces were able to enter Guca Gora without any problems. But what happened next was because of the combat activities that were taking place on the other side, we were left without any ammunition. On the other side from the direction of Zenica, Selo, Cukle sent us dramatic warnings that two-thirds of the village had already fallen, that they had a lot of wounded and dead, that they had very little supplies, and that we could expect any time that the village of Cukle fall completely. However, since we had established a line below Guca Gora, the village of Radojcici which is immediately below Guca Gora was still completely blocked, and there was a fierce fight taking place for this village. When the Croatian forces were pushed and when the village of Radojcici was deblocked, we tried to establish a defence line. However, it turned out that the quantity of ammunition that we had at our disposal was only ten bullets per one fighter. So with a huge effort and against all odds, we finally managed to establish that line.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, when did you, as a member of the command, meet with the part of the command after these combat activities?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: For days there were 24-hour operations. We had been broken up as a command, and we were split amongst various villages. And although we didn't see each other very frequently, we did not have any communication. The command post in Rudnik, in the meantime, on the 2nd of May, was shelled, and the only vehicle that we had -- that we had at our disposal had been destroyed, and any form of communication was totally disrupted. For the first time that we met but only half of the command on the 12th of June, 1993, and it was then that we got some informal information about the possible consequences of the combat activities and the developments that took place in Maline, Bikosi and the adjacent area….

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about some other events. I'm going to go back to Maline. Tell me, are you familiar with what happened in the Croatian part of the village of Miletici towards the end of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, we had problems as the brigade command with the movement across our area of responsibility. This happened immediately after the part of the command had been taken prisoner. We learned that in Mehurici after the wounding of an Arab, a group of Arabs from Mehurici started moving towards the village of Miletici and they captured some of the population. This was our initial information. However, among the captives there was the father and the uncle of one of the members of the command, who was a member of the command at the time. This person went up there, and later on we learned what had exactly happened. We learned what the general public knows today about these events that took place in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 4 and document number 5. Mr. Husic, this document, number 0915, is a document which originates from the Bosanska Krajina OG. Under item 2, does this document reflect your information, the information that you had at the time about the incident that took place in the village of Miletici?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: It does reflect that. This is a very succinct document. The -- the incident itself involved the Muslims and the Croats that were in Miletici at the time. Both these populations were captured. However, our -- after our intervention -- intervention, they were accommodated in Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document number 5, a document which originated from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Does this document describe the same incident?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The HVO document in this specific case, does it mention the persons who entered the village of Miletici exactly in the same way you were aware of the events according to the information that you received about those events?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: In this document, in the last sentence, it says: "There is knowledge that the ABiH forces are securing the village because the Mujahedin and -- various knowledge that ABiH forces are securing the village because allegedly the Mujahedin and Muslim extremists intended to burn all the houses and property in the villages." This is what it says in this HVO document. However, this does not reflect the truth, because nobody intended to burn anything, because very soon the Muslim population protected the other villagers themselves, even before the ABiH forces started protecting them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, who is -- who created this event in Maline? What did your final -- what was the final result of your investigation? Were there any members of the 306th Brigade or BH army members amongst the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: This is a document that's about Miletici and you asked me about Maline.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm asking you about Miletici.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The perpetrators of the -- this incident were exclusively foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Husic, can you please tell us about your knowledge with regard to what happened in Maline. In other words, when did you learn about these events and what did you learn about these events?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: My first information about the incidents on Bikose in Maline, I arrived on the 12th of June at a time when one part of the command met. However, the information I received at the time was that a large number of Croatian fighters were killed in the area of Bikose. At that time, the figures mentioned differed hugely. There were 10, 20, and even 30 persons mentioned. So the information was not confirmed, and we only had the complete information after the investigation that was carried out by the security organs at the time when there was already a cease-fire in place, and this was on the 14th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So what did you learn at the time? What was the result of the investigation? Who were the perpetrators of these acts?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we learned from the population, which we moved out from the area of responsibility in order to protect them, we knew from previous experiences that it was very difficult to secure the civilian population, and therefore, the members of our units took some of the people to Mehurici in order to protect them there. This is where the seat of one of the battalions was, and this is where they would have been safest. However, there were very few military policemen who were in charge of that task. They were intercepted by a group and by force, at gunpoint with the barrels of their rifles in the policemen's mouth, they took some of the Croatian population from that group. They took these people in and you known direction. It turned out that they took them from pole notes a to Maline. And at one point in time there was an incident. An incident took place. There was crying and yelling and fire was opened, and that's how these people were killed by the perpetrators still unknown to us. Their identity is still unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this is your information, but I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: These men were not able to identify the persons who had took -- taken these people away from them. They couldn't recognise them. They couldn't identify them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After the investigation what did they tell you? Were they foreigners or were they some other people?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: According to all the investigations and information, it seems that they were foreigners. However, in some reports it says that some of them were masked. And when masked persons are mentioned, then there is a doubt that these people were hiding behind their masks. We could not establish there was a single member of our unit amongst them or a member of the army to the -- for that matter, although some of the reports mentioned an interpreter. Later on when UNPROFOR investigated the incident, they established that they had a Bosniak or a Muslim among them who served as an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In line 16, page 102, it says that they were taken to Maline, and I believe that the witness said from Poljanice towards Bikose. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I told -- I said that they were take from the direction of Poljanice towards Maline and the incident took place in Bikose which is midway between Maline and Poljanice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now just a few more questions. You have told us that members of the military police, a few members of the military police, in order to provide security for the population from Maline brought these people to Mehurici. Can you please tell us whether you know where these people were accommodated? How were they treated? Who looked after them? And whether you were in any way involved and whether you monitored their lot.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. At the time when this was happening, I was engaged in combat activity. However, in the evening, I found out that a number of persons were accommodated in the primary school in Mehurici. Two persons who were members of the body for moral guidance whom I was -- to whom I was the immediate superior, who were in charge of the social and status affairs of the fighters, they informed me about that, and they were ordered to continue coordinating all the activities between the civilian protection and members of the 306th Mountain Brigade which needed to be undertaken in order to protect the population. these activities were supposed to be taken to – From then on, throughout their stay in that school, they were in charge to look after them, and they kept very meticulous record of their needs, requests, food, and everything else that was necessary. And all this time I was engaged in very intense combat activities that were taking place at the time up until the 14th. And after that, after the 14th, a special problem in the Bila valley was the destiny of the captured civilians from the village of Velika Bukovica who had been taken in an unknown direction. Their sons put a lot of pressure in order for these people to be located and returned to the area from which they had been taken. I was mostly engaged in the rescue operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to what you thought was necessary and in addition to you being aware of the fact that the army took these people to Mehurici in order to protect them, do you know how these people felt? Did they themselves ask for protection? Did you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Some of them asked not to be left in the village because they were afraid. We know what was -- what the war was like in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and. Every time after the combat activities, groups and individuals who were unruly and could not be placed under any control, and especially in the situation when the population was hungry, on the brink of starvation when there was a well known fact that there was a lot of food in Croatian villages, if civilians were to stay in such villages and disturb such groups in their rampage would put such civilians in jeopardy. That's why they asked for protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And finally, I would like to ask you whether you received any information for -- from your subordinates about bad treatment of these civilians. Did you receive any such information from an international organisation?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No, to the contrary. When they were leaving Mehurici, I came to Mehurici and since I knew some of them as my former colleagues from school, they thanked me for the care and the kindness extended to them because they were aware of the fact that they had a much better treatment, a lot more food than we ourselves had who were members of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did they have the means to go back to their villages, and did they have a free choice to join the international organisations and go back?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: At that time they did have a choice, however they decided what they decided. Their decisions were communicated. For example, they at one point in time asked from us protection to go back to their homes, to take certain valuables from their homes. We were not in a position to provide that protection because we had a very dire situation on the defence line. However, whatever request they made, we honoured those requests. One of those requests was for them to leave the area. They were escorted by UNPROFOR and went to Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Mr. Husic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any questions at this point in time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to make a break. It is 20 past four. We are going to make a 20 to 25-minute break, and we will resume in 25 minutes, at five to 5.00, and we will proceed until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said five to 4.00, but there was an error in the transcript. Can you please finish your cross-examination in about half an hour, because the Judges have some questions which will take ten to 15 minutes. Can you do it in maybe three-quarters of an hour?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will attempt to finish within 45 minutes. I hope this is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Husic. My name is Matthias Neuner. I am appearing here on behalf of the Prosecution, and as you just heard, there is limited time available. I will try to formulate the questions as precise as possible, and I would kindly ask you to answer not very lengthy, but really go to the focus at the very heart of the question. Do you understand this, please?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, you were in May 1992 in the MOS, you testified. Can you, for the benefit of the Chamber, explain what the MOS stands for? Is this the Muslimanske Snage?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness said he was never a member of the MOS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have written here down on page 85 "some other forces" and it then appeared on the transcript, "MOS".

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: That's actually why I'm asking. Could you clarify for everybody around the courtroom in May 1992 you were a member of which forces, please?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I was never a member of either HOS or MOS or any other forces save for the forces that were a legitimate continuation of the former armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So I understand, you were a member of the Territorial Defence in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Moving on to November 1992, you said you were assistant commander of morale, information, propaganda, and religious issues in the 306th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the main function such assistant commander performs? What's the main duty?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The main duties of the assistant commander for moral guidance, information propaganda and religious affairs are to provide for the functioning of combat morale in the unit. He has to provide the unit with information. He has to inform the combatants about political issues and to organise religious life. The assistant commander does that through the bodies that he has across the brigade down to the squadron level. And this is what I did. One of the most important parts of the information and training was to inform the unit about the international law and all the other principles that were to be respected in the functioning of a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You just said that you perform your activities through bodies across the brigade. Can you clarify what body or bodies you're referring to, please?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Assistant commander for morale in the command of the brigade had a team of people who were in charge of social affairs, social problems in relation to the combatants, the care for the wounded and the families of the killed, and also the information that was provided to the combatants. So these people, together with the assistant commander, were the team in charge of moral guidance. At the level of the battalion, the commanders also had assistant commanders for morale who were subordinate to the assistant commander for morale in the brigade. Together with a number of officials in charge of that, they functioned as a team. A -- company commanders also had people in charge of morale who had to convey down to the level of individual combatants whatever was necessary in terms of information, training that was conducted in those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you -- did you yourself go into combat?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So part of your function was to stay with the troop while the troop is engaged in combat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you also speak to the troops before it is leaving into combat? You give them some advice?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Every fighting involved a number of preparations whenever it was possible, including preparation in terms of morale. Unfortunately, we were too often in the situation to defend ourselves and were not in a position to actually prepare ourselves for that. But whenever it was possible, we did that during the lull in fighting or during preparations. I would go from trench to trench, and I spent most of my time with my soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said you spent most of your time with your soldiers. Does this mainly include talking to them, finding out what the status of the morale is? So is a core function of your duty talking to people within the brigade or the battalions?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And based on the information you find out by talking to people, do you later on write reports?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And these reports, do they go primarily to your brigade commander or do these reports also go to the 3rd Corps organ for information, propaganda, and religious morale?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: They went into -- in both directions. We had to submit a report on our work to our superior command and to inform them on the situation in the unit and so on and so forth. As for the other direction, towards the fighters and lower-level units, we had to inform them to the extent they needed certain information. We would inform them of that. So we did that in both directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do I understand that in the majority of the cases -- that's actually a question. In the majority of the cases you're reporting to both channels, to your brigade commander and to the 3rd Corps organ you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I would submit a report to the commander of the brigade as his assistant, the report on the situation in the units. And then as a unit, via an integral report relating to the brigade or a separate report sent to the morale organ within the corps, we would send -- we would report to the superior command, that is, the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You testified that in November 1993, you were deployed with the 3rd Corps and there the organ for information, propaganda, morale, and religious issues. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of November, 1993, I left the 306th Mountain Brigade, and after that for a while, for about three months, I was at the forward post of the Supreme Command of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whose seat was in Kakanj. After that, I arrived in the 3rd Corps and became part of the morale body within the 3rd Corps Command, and this is where I stayed until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: For how long did you remain in the forward command post in Kakanj of the Supreme Command? You said on the 30th of November you went there. For how long did you perform that function, please?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: After I reported there, I was dispatched to take care of things in the 3rd Corps. So physically I stayed actually less, for a shorter period of time than is stated in the report, because while I was doing certain things for the command of the 3rd Corps, I was still registered with the Supreme Staff in Kakanj. But I stayed for a total of three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Being then employed with the 3rd Corps in the organ for information, religious issues, propaganda, would you report there also to your commander in the 3rd Corps and also to the Supreme Command, the organ for religious affairs, morale, and propaganda there?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was responsible, first of all, to the command of the 3rd Corps. As the assistant commander, I took part in all corps-related activities. The commander of the corps was responsible to the commander of the staff of the Supreme Command, and the morale organ had his superior in the staff of the Supreme Command to whom he was answerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Coming back to the issues you would normally report, you report what you have read somewhere or especially what you have heard while visiting your troops. If I put you again in the feet of the 306 assistant commander for propaganda for information and religious morale, you would in this position report what you have heard while talking to other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: At times this would be the information that we heard from the combatants. At other times it would be just information on the events, where we were in the greater area of the Bila river valley, that we heard from civilians. So to the commander, he would convey this type of information. As for the other direction, we would inform the fighters on a general situation about the events taking place in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the international community, including the attitude of the international community towards the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How many assistant commanders were in the 306th Brigade during the time you were working there?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. The commander had assistant commander for morale, information, propaganda, and religious affairs. For financial affairs. He had assistant for logistics. Six assistants altogether so far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And one of the six commanders was the assistant commander for security affairs?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: His main responsibility was to conduct investigations if crimes occurred; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only when crimes occurred. He was in charge of the overall security situation within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So the main information sent upwards relating to security and to crimes and investigations would come from this commander or this assistant commander?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Not necessarily, because the report that was sent daily from the brigade contained separate reports on all aspects of the combat situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But the person who would be running any investigation would be the assistant commander for security affairs in the 306 Brigade?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: He would have specialised staff to do this investigation, and this staff would report to the assistant commander about the results of the investigation? The assistant commander for security appears.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to ask a few questions about the school in Mehurici. You said Mujahedin were accommodated in the school in Mehurici. In what time period were Mujahedin accommodated there?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: They were accommodated there in the fall of 1992 for a while, but when the arrival of the 1st Battalion of the 306th Brigade arrived in that school, they left it. However, a certain number of rooms and some food was left for them even after that period of time, because the building itself had been requisitioned for purposes of accommodating the army. The battalion -- actually, initially it was a detachment and then this battalion arrived, but I don't have the exact dates with respect to that. I don't know how long it lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said the Mujahedin moved out of the school to a suburb. If I understand correctly, the suburb's name of Mehurici was Poljanice.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How far away from the school is this camp or this place where the Mujahedin moved to? Is it a kilometre away, further, or less?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The term "Mujahedin" came into existence and started being used with respect to these people much later. As I have already indicated, we initially referred to them as Arabs. The largest number of them were humanitarian workers. They left to Poljanice, located only two to three kilometres from the Mehurici school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You also testified that at some point in time in 1993, Mehurici or the part held by the ABiH was hardly accessible. So basically that three sides were not accessible, but it was only possible to move out through one side. Is that correct? If so, just confirm it, please.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid we didn't understand each other. Mehurici simply could not be under that control. They were under [Realtime transcript read in error "wanted"] the control of the civilians. The Mehurici school had been commandeered for the needs of the BH army, and we controlled the school. The shelling of Mehurici by HVO, just like the shelling of all other villages, a dozen citizens, had nothing to do with BH army. We were shelled by the members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sir, I wasn't asking for the shelling, I was just asking -- you had received that --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a small correction. Line 121 -- or, rather, the page 121, line 12. The text reads, "They wanted the control," and so on. However, the witness said that the control of the village was with the civilians or, rather, that the civilians controlled the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: On page 92 of the transcript, you testified that the exits were blocked and only one -- meaning three exits. Only one exit out of the valley - not out of Mehurici, out of the valley - was basically accessible so that the population, the Muslim, mainly Muslim population could move out basically through one exit only. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No, it is not. I spoke about three exits from the Bila river valley, that is the overall territory of the area where both Bosniak and Croat populations lived. It's a geographically separate area. There were three exits, the road via Guca Gora to Travnik, the road via Zabilje towards Vitez and the road via Ovnak leading to Zenica. All three of them were blocked. So the entire valley was blocked for the free movement of the Muslim situation. Parallel to that, the Croat part of the population in 1992 while we were deployed on the line against the Chetniks had built the roads that they were able to use freely throughout that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: That's exactly what I meant. So basically the mainly Bosniak population was in this valley, couldn't move out except for one access. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: It wasn't possible for that population to use any of the route to leave the valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And I take it if it's difficult to come out of this valley - we're talking about 1993 - everybody gets to know each other very well; is that correct? The problems are shared problems in this valley?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Again I have to repeat what I already said. The Croatian population in the villages where Croatian population lived built new roads which could not be controlled by the Bosniak population. As for the Bosniak community, including both civilians and the military, in the entire valley were completely cut off from the rest of the world. They could not go through the HVO checkpoints if they didn't have permission. So it was not possible for them to move either in and out of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understood this already. I just wanted to ask if such a situation exists as you just described, this means a problem of -- doesn't this mean that the problems of the group or of some individuals are becoming problems of the whole group because the interests, the problems are shared basically? Everybody knows everybody since the only person you're depending on is the person which is in your valley.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Of course, but in all of the talks and negotiations, the civilian population, because the talks or negotiations were often mixed, negotiators were both such and military, the attitude was completely different. Their attitude was different from the attitude of the HVO. In dozens of cases they were against these blockades against us, because they were perfectly aware of the fact that that would cause major plight of the population. So Croatian civilian population in many cases opposed this activity of the HVO for the sake of the co-existence with the other community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But the units stationed in that valley knew each other since they were in the same, the ABiH units, the Mujahedin units and so on, they were in the same valley and as you said access was only possible through one exit.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Again, I think I have to correct you. Without the permission of the HVO, no one was allowed to either move in or out of the Bila river valley. No one had the authorisation to pass through. As for the units located in the Bila valley or the groups or members of other units, after all, I had been living in Sarajevo from 1973, I didn't know many of the members of these units. They didn't know me either. So we had to identify ourselves on the basis of our uniforms and the insignia, on one hand. On the other hand, members of the HVO, in particular after the establishment of the Frankopan Brigade, to be precise, after the 15th of April, in their territory had a significant number of individuals who had come from elsewhere and about whom they never wanted to talk. They never wanted to say who they were, where they had come from, but they were talking about them as their members. But for the actual members of the Frankopan Brigade, the majority of the members of the 306th knew them, and we also could tell who they were on the basis of their accent and how they spoke. And we knew who the outsiders were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there is a minor mistake but which might be significant. It's off the screen now because the witness has spoken for a while. Page 123, line 22. The transcript says "the Mujahedin units," and the witness mentioned no Mujahedin units in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to show the witness the document P664, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could the witness please look at page 2, in the middle of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: First of all, can you look at the very end, at the third page, please. Did you sign that document?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you look now at page 2, the middle of the second paragraph, and --

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Read briefly the passage dealing with Miletici. The middle of the second paragraph, just to speed up.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: "But in addition to that, an unfortunate event took place in the village of Miletici where after the wounding of one Arab with three gunshot wounds caused by 84-millimetre calibre, a group of Mujahedin, together with several people from Mehurici, quite suddenly and on their own undertook an action in which they killed five Croats and took prisoner a larger number of both Croats and Muslims."

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Who, according to this document drafted by you, who were the perpetrators? Can you please repeat this for the record?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The perpetrators of the crime were foreigners who were in this village. This document which I drafted in my capacity as official in charge of morale, on the basis of information that I received through unofficial channels is one thing. However, after the investigation, the report which was submitted later on and which can be found in the 306th Brigade gives a more precise description of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Sir, you just mentioned unofficial channels. Can you elaborate on this, please?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The way we informed the Supreme Command and the units in the other direction was based on the knowledge that we were able to gain from individual members of the units. What I knew about this event, because I was not in charge of the investigation, was based only on the information that I received from the organs from lower-level units such as battalion command. You must know that the educational level of the members of these organs was such that very few of them had completed secondary school, which was the case with the majority of the population in the Bila river valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you said you received the information from a lower-level unit such as a battalion command. Are you referring to the 306th Brigade or do you want to say that this is -- first of all, I don't understand. Is this an unofficial channel, a lower-level brigade command?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No. Assistant commander in the battalion had information, received information on the basis of what was talked about in the village. He never went to the scene of the incident, which was not my case either. He was not involved in the investigation, neither was I, but we were duty-bound to inform our superior command about the event, which was likely to have adverse effect on the units and the attitude of the units, generally speaking, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What was the name of the assistant commander, please, you were just referring to?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure who it was at the time, but I believe it was Gamal Husic. In lower-level units, the commanding officers would change quite often, so I can't be sure of the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You just said that you conveyed information which was talks about in the village. Are you referring to the village of Mehurici or in the village of -- to the village of Miletici or to another village? Which village do you mean?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Mehurici and Miletici is almost one and the same thing, because there's no distance between the two of them. The headquarters of the battalion was in Mehurici. I also said, however, that later on we received more complete information in the brigade from a member of the brigade command whose father and whose uncle had been captured. They were among the prisoners. This was the assistant commander for intelligence in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you state his name for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Dervis Suljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: On 6 May - that's the date of the document - you sent this information up to the 3rd Corps Command; is that correct? 6 May 1993.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I would like to ask the usher to show the witness another document, a new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before this document is shown I think I know what document it is, the Prosecution was kind enough to give us the document beforehand, I do wish to check if it is the same one, but we have an objection that this witness is shown that document and that the Prosecution seek to introduce that document through this witness. I will try and be as quick as possible, Your Honour, but it is an important objection to consider. Your Honour, it is the document that was shown to us at an earlier stage. If Your Honours do wish to have copies of the document so that I can address Your Honours on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Dixon, proceed please. What is your objection about? What are the reasons for your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour will immediately recognise that this is a document of a new type. We haven't had any of these kinds of documents before. They originate from the security service of the Supreme Command of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours. Sorry for the interruption, my learned friend. If I may just ask that the witness be withdrawn so that he doesn't hear all that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yeah. We have no objection if the witness stays in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the Prosecution would like the witness to leave the courtroom, so I will grant that. The Defence and the Chamber believe that this is the first time we see this type of document. Can you please indicate the origin, the source of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document comes from the ABiH collection which has been -- or this particular document has been disclosed to the Defence on the 22nd of September, 2004, and the source of this document is the Supreme Command of the ABiH armed forces. The reason why the Prosecution intends to show this document is that as the witness has just testified, he was at some point in time a member of the forward command post of the Supreme Command. He himself has sent on 6th of May a report upwards to the 3rd Corps, and this Supreme Command document dates from the 8th of May, 1993, meaning two days after the witness has sent up his report to the 3rd Corps. And the reason for showing this document to the witness would be that it also refers to Miletici, and it contains information which is partially identical with the document the witness himself has produced and partially not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, you've heard the explanation provided by the Prosecution. This document is an official document because it comes from the Supreme Command. This is a report on the situation, it seems, and we see here a chapter dedicated to the incident. And it is indicated here that there is a relation to -- there is reference to what happened in Miletici. What is your objection, Mr. Dixon?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's absolutely correct, this is an official document. However, this is not the witness, in our submission, who can comment on this document or who should be permitted to be the witness through which such a document is admitted. It is correct that he sent a report to the 3rd Corps, but there's no connection as to whether that report then went up to the security administration. But more importantly, he's not part of the Supreme Command Staff at the time. It is correct that in November, much later, this document is dated in May, much later he does become part of the command staff. But at the time, he would have had absolutely nothing to do with the preparation of this particular report. It may be that other witnesses are more appropriate to comment on what are very crucial allegations contained in this particular report, and in our submission it would be wrong for this witness to be the witness to comment on such a report. In addition to that, Your Honour, I do wish to indicate that this document was disclosed to the Defence under Rule 68 in September of this year, so after the close of the Prosecution case, and it is one, together with a number of other security service documents, high-level documents, that we are still investigating. These documents were not introduced during the Prosecution case. It wasn't expected on our part that Rule 68 material would be used in cross-examination. However, we are making, at the moment, investigations into these documents, because some of them appear to have inaccuracies in them, and it might well be that we wish to present evidence about those documents during the Defence case. So in addition to this being the wrong witness, in our view it is premature at this stage to introduce these kinds of documents, especially since they were disclosed at a very late stage to us and under Rule 68. They came in a group of documents; there were 427 of them altogether, Your Honours, totally over 1.600 pages in electronic format, and those are documents that we've only really had a month to look at and are currently reviewing. In our submission, this document should not be, at this stage, put before Your Honours. It may be that it is appropriate at a later stage. That is our application, Your Honours. I'm grateful for the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The Defence has a fundamental issue to raise, and this is whether this witness recognises -- may recognise this document since he didn't belong to the Supreme Command. And in addition to that, in the chapter dedicated to this event, there is no mention of the 306th Brigade. Have you made a note of that objection? The Defence says that this document might be introduced but not through this witness. What do you have to say to this? This witness is not in the position to recognise this document. It is beyond his authority level, and I'm -- I would like to add to that that there's no reference to the brigade to which the witness belonged at the time. I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution herself has acquired that document at a very, very late stage, so from the moment these documents arrive in the building, they still have to be scanned in. And it was virtually at the time when we got notice about this document that we were preparing for another disclosure. I can just inform you that while we are speaking, there have been more documents from this collection arrived, and the Prosecution herself had no time to look herself into these documents. They arrive on a -- I don't want to say daily basis, but in massive -- in massive batches. I note the time. It's the Prosecution's position that we have laid the foundation. We have asked the witness had the chain of command, and the witness has testified repeatedly in this section of our cross-examination that he himself had sent reports upwards or had received reports. There is, for example, one document, the Prosecution believes it's P318, which is a document which also implements on the 3rd Corps level SVK orders. So there was obviously an interplay between the two organs. For reasons of time, I just want to say that the Prosecution has compared both documents, and nine out of ten -- this is just a guess, 90 per cent of the facts are identical. They even appear to come from this document, but only in one crucial point this document -- both documents deviate, and that's the exact reason why the Prosecution wants to shed light on this. Maybe this witness can explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. We're going to withdraw for a few minutes to discuss this issue. --- Short break taken at 5.46 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has considered the issue presented by the Defence and has decided that it cannot authorise the presentation of this document because this document has to do with the presence of the 7th Brigade in Miletici. You cannot put your questions save for the possible presence of the 7th Brigade in Miletici. Please bring in the witness. Very well, then. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So has the Prosecution understood it correctly, the document can be used but the one question mentioned cannot be asked? Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only questions you may put are with regard to the presence of the brigade which is mentioned in the document. Let me resolve this. The Chamber is going to take over and ask the question. Witness, at your level, only at your level, are you aware of the fact that the supreme command of the army drafted this bulletin that had to do with the situation? Were you aware of that? Were you aware of this bulletin that was drafted by the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what bulletin do you have in mind? We received some information from the Supreme Command regarding the situation in the general area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we would forward that information to the lower-level units. Is that the bulletin that you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just show you the first page of the bulletin. Can you please tell us whether this is the type of document that you -- that you ever saw? This is the bulletin. Can you please look at the first page only.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. So you have never seen this bulletin. You do not know of its existence? You're not aware of the existence of a document of this type.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I've seen of document of this type now you've shown it to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. If in a document of this nature there is the reference to the presence of a certain member of the 7th Muslim Brigade in the area of the village of Miletici, that is of Gornji Miletici, this is the exact name that is mentioned, inhabited by the Croatian population where five villagers had been killed, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is not possible. It could not have happened, for a simple reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us the reason.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, at that time, could not have been there save for some individuals who may have been at home on leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Your rational explanation you have given us is that if this is the case, the only explanation could be that some individuals of the 7th Brigade may have been there on leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but only very few of them because members who hailed from that area were not that numerous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has answered the question, and I am giving the floor again to the Prosecution. Very well. The Prosecution, please. I think that you need additional time. Unfortunately, we will not have finished by 6.00. If interpreters cannot work longer, if they cannot work for additional 30 minutes, then we will have to work tomorrow afternoon. I would like the usher to go and see the interpreters and see if they can perhaps work for additional half an hour, and then depending on their answer, we will see whether we will have to continue tomorrow. In the meantime, I will give the floor to the Prosecution to resume their examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just to follow up what you have just responded to the Judge's question. You said there were members of the 7th on holiday. In general, was the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade or unit of such a brigade stationed in Mehurici in 1993, in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: In 1993, they couldn't have been stationed there possibly, save for a battalion of the 306th Mountain Brigade, the Siprage Battalion, nor any other unit as such. However, there were armed groups with respect to which it is very difficult to establish to whom or to what they belonged. I'm referring to individuals who during that transformation period somehow stayed behind and did not become members of any specific unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just for clarification, where were you based in April 1993, in Mehurici or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the command was located in Rudnik, in the village of -- in a mine in the village of Baja. My family, my wife and children, were in the village of Dub. So Mehurici was the place that I often went through on my way to see the family but also on my way to see the units located on Vlasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So how often did you visit Mehurici from -- either coming from Baja or from Dub? How often a month did you visit Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: At least once a week I must have passed through, but very often it was more often than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How many kilometres are the two locations away from Mehurici? I'm referring to Baja and Dub.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: Dub is located just several kilometres away in the direction of Vlasic. Baja, I couldn't tell you the exact number of kilometres. Anywhere between, I don't know, three and four. Perhaps a little more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said there were members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade groups. Do you know any names of individuals?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Brigade is not a mountain brigade, first of all. Second, speaking of the individuals, we're not talking about the groups, members of the 7th Brigade, no. There was a certain number of members of the 7th Brigade who originated from the area, who were born in the area of the Bila river valley, who were perhaps members of the 7th Brigade but who were on leave at their homes. They did not constitute any groups. They were simply individuals who were on leave for three to four days at home and who were going to go back to their unit to receive their assignments at the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see a counsel on his feet. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe the witness has clarified in his answer the issue of groups, because the answer of the Prosecutor was not phrased clearly. But I believe we have received clarification from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Interpreters have informed me that they can work for additional half an hour. They have been working since this morning, and we know how exhausting the task of interpreters is. Prosecution, how much longer do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I believe not longer than five minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Mr. Husic, you were mentioning individuals who were on leave in the Mehurici area. Do you know any names? Were these characters, these individuals known to you?

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
utterances.text: No. Well, I did know some of them by sight, but at the time it was impossible for me to know who and for how long had been a member of a particular unit. One of my very good friends, Hamid Suljic, for instance, was a member of the 7th for a while. As for others, frankly I don't know, because from 1973 until 1992, I did not live in that area. I lived in Sarajevo, a hundred kilometres away from the area in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So apart from your friend Hamid Suljic, how did you know that these individuals were members of the 7th?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We didn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you please repeat your answer? The translators didn't get your answer.

utterances.speaker: HALIM HUSIC
